title: Live: Threats of SCG walkouts as Swans men's and women's teams take the field
text:
— reporting by Lucy McNally

Polly Burridge is a self-confessed Sydney Swans tragic, and co-host of independent podcast True Bloods.

"I've been a member of the club for 20 years. It's a huge part of my life. It's probably the biggest relationship I've been in apart from my family," she said.

Polly Burridge will attend both the AFLW and AFL matches today.

But this week's Swans scandal has rocked the club, and been very tough on its biggest supporters, like Burridge.

"I always felt like they stood for the right thing, like right now I'm wearing the women's Pride guernsey — we are multicultural, inclusive, we do the best by everyone, that's why I think this has been such a shock for everyone," she said.

"When the news broke, I don't think I've ever felt so much dread. In my lifetime, we've had four grand final losses, and this was 10,000 times that. I didn't think I would ever see this crest shown in this light and I think that's why it hurt so much."

But despite the pain, Burridge is planning to go to today's double-header; to watch both the men's and women's matches.

"At one point during this week I thought I'd just go for the girls then leave because it was at the point where the sanctions had not been handed down," she says.

"But now that the club has decided, I don't think it's fair to punish the boys who have done nothing wrong as they have also had their trust broken."

Polly Burridge is co-host of independent podcast True Bloods.

The Swans AFLW team play Essendon Bombers today.

Their coach Colin O'Riordan held a press conference on Friday alongside captain Lucy McEvoy, where he expressed his disappointment over the scandal, as well as his deep pride in the women's side.

McEvoy was then asked how she and her teammates were coping.

Polly Burridge said it's a shame the AFLW side has to deal with those questions.

"I understand why people want a women's perspective on this but at the same time they are still professionals, they still have a game to play and you need to let them do their job as opposed to being the beacon of hope for everyone," she said.

"Yes let's interview Callum Mills, let's not necessarily interview Lucy McEvoy, let's let her do her job and ask her a question about the football rather than 'how do you feel about the segregation between the two teams?'"

The podcast host said she is now excited to head to Moore Park today.

"I do think the girls will absolutely win … I do think they'll have a fantastic game," Burridge said.

"I think the boys who have been hurt are going to put in a good show. It's going to be a beautiful day of unity, a day the Swans fans will remember forever."

title: NT government pursues Fair Work action over firefighters, corrections dispute
text:
After more than a year of bargaining with the union representing firefighters and correctional officers, the NT government has filed two applications to the Fair Work Commission (FWC) in a move that could jeopardise its own public sector wages policy.

Earlier this year, the Commissioner for Public Employment applied to the FWC for two separate intractable bargaining declarations.

Under Commonwealth law, an intractable bargaining declaration could lead to the FWC independently deciding pay and conditions for workers, potentially forcing the government to abandon its policy of maximum 3 per cent wage rises for public sector workers.

The United Workers Union Northern Territory (UWU NT), which represents both firefighters and correctional officers, has challenged the applications, accusing the government of neglecting its duty.

"The government is not focusing on real negotiation and trying to improve public sector workers' conditions of employment," UWU NT secretary Erina Early said.

Erina Early says the government has not engaged in "real negotiation" but the commissioner for public employment disagrees. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

"They're more focused on litigation and legal proceedings."

But Commissioner for Public Employment Nicole Hurwood defended the applications.

In a statement, she said the UWU has rejected multiple offers for new enterprise agreements, including some informed by the FWC's recommendations.

Nicole Hurwood says the government's applications to the Fair Work Commission were necessary. (ABC News: Hamish Harty)

"The government has been clear with the UWU about the fiscal parameters within which it can negotiate," her statement read.

" The union continues to pursue claims that are significantly beyond what the government considers affordable or reasonable. "

Edith Cowan University lecturer in industrial relations Dr Alexis Vassiley said it was unusual to see governments applying for intractable bargaining declarations due to their unpredictable outcomes.

Alexis Vassiley says it is possible the FWC could give workers more than the 3 per cent pay rise. (ABC News: West Matteeussen)

"It's risky because what it does do is take the dispute out of the hands of the parties," he said.

"The Fair Work Commission isn't bound by the NT government's wages policy, so they could rule in favour of a much higher than 3 per cent increase."

Questions over cost as bargaining agreements bank up

Corrections officers and firefighters are two of seven workforces currently negotiating new enterprise agreements with the NT government.

The government is also negotiating with NT medical officers, dentists, nurses and midwives, Territory Generation and Power and Water Corporation employees.

Electrical Trades Union Northern Territory (ETU NT) organiser David Hayes said the pay offers made to Territory Generation and the Power and Water Corporation staff were "a joke."

"We've been offered a 2.75 per cent pay increase per year across the board, which is an absolute insult to those workforces," he said.

Union representatives Brendan Bussenschutt, David Hayes, Heidi Crisp and Erina Early are all fighting for better pay for workers. (ABC News: Tristan Hooft)

Australian Nursing and Midwifery Federation (ANMF) NT branch secretary Heidi Crisp said the policy of 3 per cent annual wage rises would hamper workforce numbers.

"People are having to resort to either being agency nurses or doing excessive overtime just to pay their regular bills," she said.

The ANMF NT is instead pursuing a 20.5 per cent wage increase over the next three years.

For union leaders such as Mr Hayes and Ms Crisp, the NT government's applications for intractable bargaining declarations involving corrections officers and firefighters set a worrying precedent.

The verdict on the application to the FWC for correctional officers will be handed down on September 2. (ABC News: Grace Atta)

Ms Early said pursuing this action against unions would be fiscally irresponsible.

"For the intractable bargaining process, [the government is] spending a lot of money on interstate lawyers to go up against firefighters and corrections officers," she said.

"This government has money to fight workers, but they have no money to invest in workers?"

The verdict on the application to the FWC for NT firefighters is set to be delivered on Wednesday. (ABC News: Mitch Woolnough)

In a statement, Ms Hurwood said the government was yet to spend any money on lawyers for its FWC hearings.

"No legal costs have been incurred to date, as the intractable bargaining declaration processes have only recently commenced," the statement read.

"Legal representation will be required as the matters progress, with the associated costs borne by the relevant agencies."

The FWC will hand down its verdict on the intractable bargaining declaration application for NT firefighters this Wednesday, August 26, while their verdict on corrections officers will be handed down on September 2.

title: Grafton 12yo takes campaign to politicians to fix beloved skate park
text:
When 12-year-old Haylee Blair found a problem that needed fixing, she decided to take action.

The avid skater from South Grafton, in northern NSW, was dismayed at the state of her local skate park.

"There's cracks and holes everywhere and glass and stuff all over the skate park," she said.

"I love skateboarding and it's a skate park for a reason, but we're using it as a bike track because it's too rough."



The Grafton Skate Park was first built in 1998, with expansions undertaken in 2001 and 2011.



The Clarence Valley Council's 2021 Draft Plan of Management for the skate park and other facilities noted the bowls had aged and its poor condition presented a safety hazard to users.

Haylee is a keen and active skater but says the Grafton park is not fit for purpose. (Supplied: Trudi Blair)

Haylee has a vision for a brighter future, and has been using the power of democracy to make it happen.

This week, she approached her local council and asked for action to deliver the much-needed maintenance.

"Our park is used by so many young people, and it means a lot to our community," she wrote.

The cracks and debris at the skate park are unsafe for skateboarders to ride over, Haylee says. (Supplied: Trudi Blair)

On Thursday, the council voted unanimously to take up Haylee's cause, with a staff report to be brought back before councillors by October.



Councillor Cristie Yager called for the report and put Haylee’s case to the council.



“Haylee and her family and now a very large group of people are getting behind the positivity that would come from having the skate park brought back up to a standard where it is suitable for skating," Cr Yager said at the council meeting on Thursday.



“I’m hoping we can get a whole lot of information that is available publicly that can help us find any kind of avenue forward on getting [the skate park] up to scratch.”



Cr Yager said that the upgrades to the Grafton skate park may not happen within this term of council.



Haylee said her desire is for future repairs to the park to have some additions to help skaters of all ages take up the sport.

"I would like to see a smoother skate park and maybe … a pump track for littler kids to have a go, because currently the ramps are way too big for little kids," she said.

"[Also some] shading and cameras."

It has been a sustained effort by the young skater, who first brought the issue to light on the community radio program she hosts after school.

That led to an invitation to present to a local rotary club, and then last month a conversation with her local mayor and member for state parliament.

Haylee is celebrating the council's vote. (Supplied: Trudi Blair)

Although supportive, Cr Ray Smith said the council did not have the funds for the estimated $250,000 project, and would need government assistance to pay for the work.

'That's community'

A little north from Haylee's hometown, the nearby regional city of Lismore shows how transformative a skate park can be.

Since opening a new state-of-the-art facility last August, Lismore has hosted several major skate events, including an official Skate Australia Olympic pathway event in April.

Even when major events are not running, the park is rarely empty.

Lismore's new skate park was widely anticipated and has been popular since it opened in 2025. (Supplied: Lismore City Council)

"I start coaching down there at 7:30 most mornings, and I'm always surprised, sometimes there's people there skating even before I get there," skate coach and skate shop owner Samual Izac said.

"And then into the evening, I'll be coaching two, three sessions in a row and then people keep turning up until the lights go off at 11."

Mr Izac said there were skaters as young as three or four, through to adults into their 50s.

"When you're bringing people of all ages and demographics together socially, that's a really good thing," he said.

"To me, that's community."

Samual Izak says a good skate park brings the community together. (Supplied: Lismore City Council)

Haylee hopes a refurbished or perhaps even a rebuilt skate park in Grafton could bring her own community together, especially younger people.

"It's so they can get out, have fun for free, exercise and get off their phones," she said.

title: Breaking: Australia records its first bird flu case in a mammal
text:
Australia's first case of bird flu in a mammal has been confirmed following testing of a long-nosed fur seal found in South Australia.

Federal Agriculture Minister Julie Collins has told reporters in Hobart the seal was found at Beachport, 300 kilometres south of Adelaide.

"This is sadly our first confirmed case of H5 bird flu in a mammal in Australia," Ms Collins said.

"Although this is a concerning development, it is not unexpected for us to start to see infection in other wildlife, particularly in marine mammals, particularly in areas where there are high infection rates in wild birds.

"I have been advised that at this time the detection does not appear to be associated with other sick or dead marine mammals.

"An infection of this individual animal is likely to have occurred due to exposure to infected wild birds or the environment that they share."

Julie Collins announced the confirmed case at a media conference in Hobart. (ABC News)

There have now been 298 positive H5 bird flu events recorded in Australia since the outbreak, with 183 of those in South Australia.

"At this stage there is no evidence of infection in our poultry or agriculture systems," Ms Collins said.

The minister said she would be travelling to South Australia "in the coming days" to discuss the state's response to H5 bird flu.

She urged anyone who sees sick or dead birds not to touch them or get close to them but to record their location and make a report.

title: One Nation pursuing migration rate 'not too different' to Labor
text:
One Nation MP David Farley says immigration rates to Australia would not be "too different" to Labor or the Coalition under Pauline Hanson, as he suggested a figure close to the government's migration target of 225,000 by 2028.

Mr Farley told ABC Insiders One Nation would not seek to cut migration rates deeper than about 230,000 a year, saying the migration target would be a net overseas migration rate of about 130,000 plus "a minimum" 100,000 skilled workers under established visa schemes.

The net overseas migration (NOM) rate accounts for the total number of people entering Australia with plans to stay at least a year minus those leaving, including those entering on visa programs such as working holiday-maker visas, the Pacific Australia Labour Mobility scheme, and skilled worker visas.

Mr Farley admitted once One Nation's "true NOM" and skilled visa targets were combined, its migration rate of about 230,000 would be similar to figures already forecast by the government.

"The raw number is not too different, but the reality is where do we need them. We don't need them in the great urban 'metroplex'. We need them out to be productive, working out in agriculture, engineering, mining, etc," Mr Farley said.

"The big difference is we are focusing on what are the skills we need as a nation."

Everybody wants to cut migration The causes of migration are murky and it is harder for politicians to control than they would like to admit.

Mr Farley said One Nation was focused on net migration "in its true form", plus workers from several necessary visa programs, citing about 40,000 migrants under the Pacific workers visa, about 68,000 to 70,000 skilled aged care migrants and skilled mechanical and engineering workers.

He said that category would make up "a minimum" of 100,000 more visas granted each year under a One Nation government, on top of what he described as the "true" net overseas migration rate of 130,000.

While the government has forecast migration returning to about 225,000 by 2028, it has repeatedly overshot those forecasts, particularly after the reopening of international borders following the COVID-19 pandemic.

The One Nation MP's comments follow weeks of debate on how deeply migration rates should be cut, an issue that has become a political battleground in part because of One Nation's rise in popularity on a platform of slashing migration.

The party has also laid out its intentions to restrict migration from some countries deemed to be higher risk, suggesting it could use travel advice to determine which countries should be affected by migration restrictions.

The Coalition has been developing a migration policy to combat One Nation, as the right wing party has emerged from the fringe of politics to threaten the Coalition's status as the opposition.

While it has not yet set migration targets, the Coalition intends to tie migration to housing construction rates, saying that migration rates will be restricted to the pace of housing completions in the previous year in order to close the supply shortfall in the housing sector.

The government, meanwhile, has been planning reforms to further tightening of temporary visas as it seeks to bring down net overseas migration from 300,000 to its goal of 225,000 by 2028.

Those reforms were postponed, with the policy still to be settled by cabinet.

In July, the government issued a directive to prioritise people already onshore for visa processing, slowing arrivals overseas — including for in-demand skilled workers in nursing, teaching and elsewhere.

Business fears race to bottom on migration

With both major parties and One Nation competing on migration, business groups have stepped up their calls for "stability" in the migration system, fearing a race to the bottom could leave industries with deeper worker shortages.

On Friday, the Australian Industry Group said skilled migration was "essential" to addressing workforce shortages in housing, infrastructure, manufacturing, health, aged care and in emerging industries.

"Australia cannot meet current and future workforce needs through domestic training alone," chief executive Innes Willox said.

"Reducing skilled migration at a time of persistent workforce shortages would put further pressure on housing delivery, major infrastructure projects and business investment."

The industry group urged that permanent skilled migration remain at current levels, and asked for visa processing and skills recognition processes to be sped up.

It also asked for the government to do more to explain to voters how migration supports essential services and the economy.

title: $20m avocado packing shed upgrade halves workforce with robots
text:
In a nondescript fruit packing shed in regional Western Australia, nine giant Japanese-made robots demonstrate their skills.

The huge machines are scanning, stacking and shifting pallets of avocadoes.

These jobs used to be carried out by humans, but automation has allowed the Avocado Collective in Manjimup, 300 kilometres south of Perth, to halve its casual workforce while doubling its production capacity.

The collective has invested $17 million into its robot workforce amid high labour costs and fears of changes to overseas worker schemes.

Growers say they embraced the decision to turn to automation, with local staff becoming harder to find.

But unions and labour experts have mixed feelings about the impact of robots.

Avocados at a nearby farm in Pemberton. (Supplied: Russell Delroy)

Advantages to automation

Avocado Collective operations manager Craig Boyce said the machines had many advantages, particularly reliability and workplace safety.

"They turn up to work every day, don't complain about a sore back, there are no health and safety issues, and you can load them up," he said.

Mr Boyce said the Japanese-built machines replaced between 40 and 50 staff at the South West-based operations across a range of roles.

"Realistically, we're talking everyone who hand stacks [pallets], everyone who scans, and everyone who drives forklifts," he said.

Craig Boyce says robots are changing the industry. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

The collective, which describes itself as the largest packing facility in Australia, said the robots were part of a broader $20 million investment in automation.

The combination of high-volume crops and increasing domestic demands has created ideal conditions for significant investment.

It said three quarters of operations at the facility were now automated, more than doubling its potential weekly output from 1 million kilograms to 2.52 million.

Workers still manually pack trays of avocados. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Mr Boyce said automation was a key part of reducing costs.

"You'll never replace everyone because you still need a level of management and maintenance," he said.

"But obviously the cost of labour is an ever-increasing phenomena."

The nine robots can process 2.5 million kilograms of avocados a week. (Supplied: Avocado Collective)

Local workers hard to find

Manjimup has become heavily reliant on migrant workers through the federal government's Pacific Australia Labour Mobility (PALM) Scheme, with an estimated 400 working in the region.

Pemberton avocado grower Dean French, a director at the collective, said PALM workers were still welcomed and valued.

Dean French says finding workers is a constant challenge. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

However, automation reduced dependence on the government scheme.

"It probably sounds like a dystopian nightmare that we are not employing people," Mr French said.

"But it means we don’t have to bring people in from overseas. We find it very difficult to get locals to work."

The horticulture industry says workers are increasingly hard to find. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Fellow grower George Ipsen dismissed the idea robots were depriving people of jobs.

"We can't get workers, we import labour from the Pacific Islands, and East Timor," he said.

Mr Ipsen said he was also concerned the federal government could change the PALM system, after it slowed backpacker visas.

"It would destroy the industry here," he said.

Each of the nine robots was built in Japan and moves and stacks pallets of fruit. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Unions, academic express concerns

But not everybody sees robots in the avocado industry as good news.

UnionsWA secretary Rikki Hendon called for greater guardrails to protect workers.

"Automation may make businesses more profitable, but much of the evidence points to it making our communities poorer," she said.

University of Sydney work and labour market professor Chris Wright accepted automation could alleviate health and safety concerns.

A sign out at the front of the Avocado Collective. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

"But it would also mean the elimination of jobs and that can affect livelihoods and their ability to support themselves," he said.

Professor Wright said automation could help create more skilled jobs, but did not benefit casuals or PALM workers.

"It's really imperative for the businesses, and for governments, to ensure workers are supported as part of that transition," he said.

The Australian Government provides employers up to $600 for each PALM worker for job specific training, and said the program helped strenthen participants' long-term employability.

Human workers here to stay

However, Mr Boyce said automation created opportunities for the local workforce.

"We've taken them from forklift drivers to robotic technicians; we actually upped their game," he said.

Avocados being sorted in Manjimup. (ABC News: Georgia Loney)

Avocados Australia chairman Brad Rogers said the PALM scheme would continue to be important to the avocado industry.

"I really don't see that changing anytime soon, because some strong relationships have been built over the years," he said.

" Physical labour is going to be around for a very long time. "

The Australian government said it remained committed to the PALM scheme and to ensuring the safety, welfare and wellbeing of workers.

title: I gave birth to my twin brother's baby and saved his life in the process
text:
Twins Adam Braitberg and Ellie Freeman grew up in what they describe as a loving and close-knit family in suburban Melbourne/Naarm.

That bond has only grown stronger since Ellie and eldest sister Jess helped Adam and his husband Omer Kuchman bring daughter Gali into the world.

Whether it's romantic, platonic, heartbreaking or surprising, our Love Story series is about love in all its forms. Share yours with us.

These are Ellie and Adam's words.

We were a very close-knit Jewish family

Ellie: We had a beautiful upbringing in suburban Melbourne with our parents and two sisters. We constantly had a revolving door of friends and family and every Friday night we'd have massive Sabbath meals with our four grandparents and aunties and uncles.

Ellie and Adam (bottom left and right) had an idyllic upbringing in suburban Melbourne with their sisters Jess and Romy. (Supplied)

Adam: We were a very close-knit Jewish family. .

I moved overseas when I was 23 and I moved back [to Australia] three months ago. We managed to keep this close relationship from long distance, as well as with all my sisters and their kids. I'm very close with my nieces and nephews, even though none of them grew up around me.

'I'm here for you, forever'

Adam: I told Ellie I was gay when I was 19.

I got very nervous but she was like, "Wow, that's amazing. " The biggest homophobia is always internal; you're always more worried about how you'll be perceived than what the reality is.

Jess, Romy, Ellie and Adam have managed to stay close despite geographical separation. (Supplied: Corey Wright photography)

Ellie: I was so proud that he was in a space where he'd accepted it and wanted to share it, because it's such a big part of your identity, hiding it would be an awful feeling. I remember saying, "I'm here for you, forever."

When Omer met Adam — and his family

Adam: Omer and I have been together for four years. He's originally from Israel. Introducing him to the family was a very big step. It was my grandmother's 90th birthday and we all went to a resort together in Thailand. It was my sisters, my grandmother, my aunties and uncles; 37 people.

Ellie: We all loved Omer straight away. When we were in Thailand, Adam and Omer announced that they were engaged, so the natural conversation about children began. Our eldest sister, Jess, offered to be a surrogate first and said she'd also be happy to be an egg donor.

Under Australian law, you can't be both, so it worked out that my sister was happy to be the egg donor and I was happy to be a surrogate.

'Shit, he's got cancer'

Ellie: I got routine surrogacy blood tests before the process started and my husband, Elliot, who's a gastroenterologist, looked at the bloods and said, "Hang on, Ellie, this is the lowest your ferritin has ever been; you shouldn't be this low."

He said, "You need to a colonoscopy and gastroscopy to check everything's OK before you start the surrogacy process". So, I did, and they found 21 polyps in my colon. Polyps can turn cancerous, so it meant my first-degree relatives needed a colonoscopy, just to rule it out for themselves.

'If you need my kidney, take it' Despite a 10-year age gap and geographical separation, Sajarn and Codey Stow have retained a close bond since childhood. That bond has only strengthened since Codey received a donor kidney from his brother last November.

Adam: Omer and I had a wedding in Israel last year and the whole family came and it was beautiful. Ellie told us [about the polyps] just before, so I booked in for a month later for my colonoscopy and [discovered] I also had polyps, and I also had a 10-centimetre mass … I had cancer. Ellie had to inform the nurses, which meant the process had to stop temporarily to make sure I was healthy.

Ellie: Adam found out he had colon cancer on a Thursday and my first [embryo] implantation was meant to be the following day and then Adam sent us the report and my husband and I were like, "Shit, he's got cancer."

Adam: We found a doctor in Jerusalem who managed to see me and a month later, I had a surgery. Then tests, follow-ups, and I'm clear, I'm in remission. A month later, Ellie fell pregnant with our baby.

Ellie: Had the surrogacy not happened, I wouldn't have known I have that [polyposis] syndrome and Adam potentially wouldn't have found that cancer.

Adam: This baby pretty much — both emotionally and physically — saved our lives.

Gali's birth brought us closer

Ellie: I said to my three kids, "Next time Mummy is pregnant, I'm helping Adam and Omer create a family, so it's not going to be our baby, it'll be your little cousin".

It was a beautiful birth. To have my husband by my side the whole time was the most important thing for me.

Ellie says Gali is a special girl "for many, many reasons" and has made Adam and her even closer. (Supplied)

I birthed Gali differently [to my own children]. She was in Adam's hands straight away, [whereas] my babies are usually put straight onto me. Gali went straight to Adam and Omer, they cut the cord and it was the most beautiful thing.

I didn't know what postpartum looks like when you don't have a baby with you. It was much the same in terms of the emotional hormonal rollercoaster. But it was never a question of, "Where's the baby that I birthed?" Because I saw her go to her parents and I didn't ever have that connection; I truly didn't.

Adam: I don't think the dynamic itself between us has changed, but I think there's something different. I have three sisters who each have three kids and I'm also a parent now. All four Braitberg kids are parents.

When we were younger, people used to refer to us as like the Brady Bunch family, because we were super close, and you don't get much closer than this, right? Gali is a beautiful baby and she's also a beautiful symbol of what family is and what family could be.

Adam and Ellie's elder sister Jess Sztrajt, who was the egg donor for the surrogacy, nurses a newborn Gali. (Supplied)

Ellie: It's brought us together and strengthened that bond that was always there. How can it not? Gali's a really special girl for many, many reasons. The fact we've been able to do this has definitely strengthened the love we have for all of us.

Adam: For Gali, she's going to know, it's not something to hide from her. [We'll tell her] "This is how you were created; you have two incredible aunties that wanted you to exist so much they helped us create you."

title: Pogačar hails rival after 'unimaginable' week following brother's death
text:
Tadej Pogačar has delivered an ominous and stunning start to the Vuelta a España, edging British rider Ethan Hayter by just 0.09 seconds in the opening stage time trial.

However, the world number one said after the race that he had hoped Britain's Josh Tarling would come out on top.

Tarling was competing in the Vuelta just days after his brother Finlay Tarling was killed when he was hit by a non-accredited car on the course during the Volta a Portugal.

Competing despite his brother's death, Tarling delivered a blistering time of his own to be well in contention for stage honours.

As it happened, Soudal Quick-Step's Hayter finished four seconds faster than his grieving compatriot, with Pogačar pipping them both, before saying it would have been fitting had Tarling claimed victory.

"When I was going to the start line, I saw that Josh has the best time and, I really wish he wins today," Pogačar said at the finish.

"For sure I would do my best, but it was also this kind of strange moment. I was really rooting, myself, for Josh.

"Then I came to the intermediate [time check] and I hear a different name [over the radio], I hear Ethan Hayter was ahead of me by three seconds and I say, 'OK, I give it my all but no risks' and then we'll see what happens.

"I would really like to see Josh do well at this Vuelta."

Tarling's Netcompany INEOS director sportif Geraint Thomas was also full of praise for Tarling.

"It's been great to have him here. He was really keen to ride and wanted to get back to the day job and find comfort in the process and be around the team to be a normal as possible," fellow Welshman Thomas said.

"It's been unimaginable what he's gone through this last week or so.

Josh Tarling was awarded the white jersey as the race's Most Combative Rider after the first stage. (Getty Images: Tim de Waele)

"To put in a performance like that at the end of the week or so is just fantastic and shows the class of him as person and an athlete, so [we] couldn't be prouder.

"I think the course suited him technically. He's one of the best and yesterday was probably the first time he's ridden a bike properly in a while, so to still put that in is insane, really.

"We'll just continue to be normal around him now and support as best we can."

Tarling's parents, Michael and Dawn, had both given their eldest son their blessing to compete at the Vuelta, saying it was what his brother would have wanted.

"Finlay was so incredibly proud of his big brother, and would be watching, nose to the TV and shouting as he competed," they wrote in a post on social media.

"So it is right that Josh honours that love."

Pogačar, who's bidding to become just the ninth men's rider to win all three Grand Tours in their career, put himself in position from the offset by completing the highly technical 9.5-kilometre course through the streets of Monaco — where he resides — in 10 minutes, 57 seconds.

Pogačar is competing at the Vuelta for the first time since making his Grand Tour debut as a 20-year-old in the 2019 race. He won three stages and finished third, which incredibly is his worst overall result in the three-week events.

This year is going much better, though.

Why these people believe in 'freak' Pogačar's victories As Tadej Pogačar continues to mop up cycling's biggest accolades and most controversial record, one former doper believes he's found the answer to his success: he is just a "freak".

Pogačar won the Tour de France for the third-straight time to claim his fifth overall title in July, equalling the record for the most overall wins at the race.

The two-time reigning world champion also won the Tour de Suisse and Tour de Romandie stage races as well as celebrating victories at three of the year's one-day monument races — Liège-Bastogne-Liège, the Ronde van Vlaanderen and Milano-Sanremo — while finishing second in the other, Paris-Roubaix.

He also claimed victory in Strade Bianche and has now finished first in 17 of the 38 race days he has completed in 2026.

Pogačar won the Giro d'Italia at the first attempt in 2024, so the Vuelta is the only Grand Tour race he is yet to conquer.

The only other men to have won all three are Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault, Jacques Anquetil, Alberto Contador, Chris Froome, Felice Gimondi, Vincenzo Nibali and his long-time rival, Jonas Vingegaard.

The win was Pogačar's first in the opening stage of a Grand Tour, and it's also the first time he took the red jersey as the Vuelta leader. It's his 36th Grand Tour stage win altogether.

No man has led the Vuelta from start to finish since Swiss legend Tony Rominger did so during the 1994 race.

Such a feat has only happened eight times in men's grand tour history, three times at the Vuelta.

Merckx, the man to whom Pogačar is so often compared, managed the feat once too, at the 1973 Giro d'Italia.

Pogačar's main rival, Vingegaard, is not racing at the 81st edition of the Vuelta as he recovers from a broken collarbone sustained in a crash the day after he was woken at 2am for a doping test at the Tour de France.

Remco Evenepoel, who finished second behind Pogačar at the Tour, is also not competing. The Belgian rider has opted for rest and specific training for the Road World Championships in Montréal next month.

Monaco became the first city to host the start of all three Grand Tours. The Giro d'Italia started in the principality in 1966 and it staged the start of the Tour de France in 2009.

Much of the time trial route on Saturday covered the same course as the annual Formula 1 Grand Prix.

The second stage will also start in Monaco before a 214.3km hilly trek through Provence to Manosque. It will be the longest stage of the race, which finishes in the southern Spanish city of Granada on September 13.

title: Teen Socceroo makes perfect EPL debut with win over Manchester United
text:
Teenage Socceroo Lucas Herrington has made a dream start to life in the Premier League, coming on as a second-half substitute in Hull City's boilover 2-0 victory over giants Manchester United.

The 18-year-old defender, the only Australian in English soccer's top-flight, didn't put a foot wrong in promoted Hull's return to the big-time when he came on to help them protect their two-goal lead.

The lanky Queenslander was immaculate at the heart of the home side's defence for the final half-hour as Hull confounded all the doubters to earn their first league victory over United in 52 years.

Written off as overwhelming relegation favourites, the Yorkshire side were well worth their win over a lumbering United, whose build-up play was too pedestrian and attacking execution too shoddy.

In the 38th minute the Tigers' central defender Nobel Mendy, who was signed on the same day as Herrington earlier in the month but who got the nod to start ahead of the young Aussie, scored their second goal.

By that time, Michael Carrick's United were already struggling to get to grips with a side that deservedly led through a couple of first-half set-pieces.

Centre-back Semi Ajayi opened the scoring in the 17th minute when United failed to deal with a corner, and then Regan Slater whipped in a 38th minute free-kick that Mendy latched on to, nodding home expertly.

But when Mendy had to come off injured in the 64th minute, Herrington, a record $A33 million signing for an Australian player, got his big moment, the former Colorado Rapids defender coming on in a triple substitution.

He became the first Australian teenager to play in the Premier League since Harry Kewell and, at 18 years 351 days, is the third-youngest Australian to play in England's top-flight.

The youngster with a big reputation for his calmness never looked fazed as United tried to eke their way back into the match with a series of largely lumbering attacks.

He only had nine touches amid United's huff-and-puff but they all told of a lad who already seems at home in this elevated company.

With Hull's Bosnian boss, Sergej Jakirovic, revealing Ajayi, Mendy and captain Lewis Coyle will all have to be assessed for their injuries over the next 24 hours, Herrington will next be in line to feature in Wednesday morning's AEST League Cup tie at Championship side Stoke.

Then he may well feature in their next league game, a huge one at also-promoted Coventry, who lost their opener on Friday 3-0 at champions Arsenal.

title: US imposes visa bonds of up to $27k for several Pacific countries
text:
Clients never used to cry in Alisi Mo'ungaloa Afu's office, but it's not uncommon these days.

"Some people have cried because they weren't able to travel to funerals," she said.

Mrs Mo'ungaloa Afu is a Tonga-based travel agent who has spent 15 years helping locals navigate the United States visa process.

Many Tongans have family in the US and travel there to attend weddings, funerals or reunite with loved ones.

Alisi Mo'ungaloa Afu is a travel agent who specialises in US visa applications. (Supplied)

Mrs Mo'ungaloa Afu helps clients prepare application forms, pay fees and schedule and prepare interviews with a consulate officer.

For Tongans, it is an expensive process.

The US embassy in Tonga doesn't offer visa application services, so applicants usually have to travel to nearby Fiji for their visa interview, which involves additional travel costs and time away from work.

An interview does not guarantee a visa, nor is the $US185 ($260) visa application fee refundable.

Tongan applicants usually need to travel to Suva in Fiji for their US visa interview. (Supplied)

At the start of this year, a pilot US Visa Bond Program was introduced, under which applicants from Tonga and 37 other countries had to pay a bond of between $US5,000 ($7,000) and $US15,000 before a visa can be issued.

The program is aimed at curbing "overstays" and applies to non-immigrant applicants seeking B1 and B2 visas, which are the primary visas issued for business and tourism travel in Tonga.

The amount depended on the applicant's "personal circumstances" and is refundable if the traveller meets all visa conditions.

However, that bond has now become even more expensive, increasing to a range of $US10,000 ($14,000) to $US20,000 ($27,000) after the pilot project was made permanent on August 3.

Passport holders from 50 countries, including Tonga, Fiji, Tuvalu and Papua New Guinea, are subject to the program.

Tongans often fly to the US to visit friends and family in the Tongan diaspora community. (Reuters)

The rules also apply to nationals of those countries living in Australia.

This means Tongans or Fijians who are permanent residents of Australia could still be subject to the bond if they apply for a US visa using their Pacific Island passport.

The US State Department states the requirement applies "regardless of place of application".

'$US20k is what someone makes in a year'

Tonga's prime minister, Lord Fakafanua, said the program being made permanent was very disappointing, and he would look at diplomatic solutions to have the restrictions alleviated.

"It's very close to home because of our large diaspora in places like California, Hawaii and Utah and we are actively working on remedying it," he said.

Lord Fakafanua said he would look at diplomatic solutions to have travel restrictions on Tonga alleviated. (Supplied)

About 78,000 people are part of the Tongan diaspora in the US, according to the most recent US census.

Mrs Mo'ungaloa Afu's mother and siblings are among that figure, as are the friends and relatives of the 500 to 600 clients she typically helps each year.

She said business had "plummeted" after the pilot bond program was introduced in January because many of her clients couldn't afford the application fee, travel cost, and the bond.

She said none of her clients had travelled to the US since.

Alisi Mo'ungaloa Afu said many Tongans would not be able to afford the bond. (ABC News: Nick Sas)

"We have seen significant decline in our people wanting to apply for a US visa, just because of the expenses alone," she said.

Mrs Mo'ungaloa Afu said even the minimum bond of $US10,000 would be out of reach for many Tongans, particularly those living inside the Kingdom.

"$US20,000 is about what someone makes in a year or two years of income in Tonga," she said.

Before the program, Mrs Mo'ungaloa Afu said she typically travelled to the US once a year to visit her siblings and aging mother.

She paid thousands in airfares for her family of six to travel to the US around Christmas last year.

She said a bond would make future trips virtually impossible.

"Right now, the priority is to just get a visa in case something happens like a funeral," she said.

"That is the main reason I'd want to travel."

Curbing overstay

Jope Tarai said only very well-to-do Fijians would be able to afford to pay a visa bond to holiday in the US. (Reuters)

Fijian political analyst Jope Tarai said the program reflected anti-immigration sentiment that could make other parts of the world more appealing to Pacific Islanders.

"One of those places for Fijian passport holders is China," he said.

"It's visa-free entry, so this is going to have huge implications between two big competing powers in certain parts of the region, so far as soft power is concerned."

Jope Tarai. (ABC News)

The US State Department said the Visa Bond Program had dramatically improved overstay trends, and that 98 per cent of the 5,000 travellers who were issued visas with bonds returned to their country on time during the 12-month pilot period.

Previously, official figures list Tonga's B-1 and B-2 overstay rate at 6.45 per cent, while it's estimated 14 per cent of Tongan students overstay their visas.

Like Tonga, Fiji has a large diaspora in the US with about 54,000 people identifying as Fijian. But it has a lower overstay rate of 3.95 per cent, according to official figures.

ICE agents in the US have been targeting visa overstayers in cities across the US. (Reuters)

Vanuatu and Tuvalu meanwhile have much smaller US diaspora communities than Tonga and Fiji.

Henrietta McNeill-Stowers, a research fellow at the Australian National University's Department of Pacific Affairs, said Tuvalu's high overstay rate (11.63 per cent) may explain why it's part of the Visa Bond Program.

However, other factors may have played a role for PNG and Vanuatu citizens being subjected to the bond.

"For Vanuatu, some of it is around identity verification and travel document security," she said.

"Their citizenship by investment scheme is something the US is keeping an eye on."

title: 'Most people wouldn't even realise': Why Canberra is a data centre hotspot
text:
Many might not have noticed they are there, but facilities on industrial estates across Canberra — and in at least one instance in the suburbs at Bruce — are housing vast amounts of data and increasingly AI.

The ACT government estimates there are already 15 data centres in Canberra, and says there are proposals for a new one in Beard, as well as a possible extension to another in Hume.

CDC Data Centres operates eight data centres across four campuses in the ACT, employing about 250 people.

The company's chief executive, Greg Boorer, set up their first data centre in Canberra in 2007.

CDC Data Centres CEO Greg Boorer says investment in renewable energy generation and "closed-loop" cooling systems have helped allay local community concerns about data centres. (Harry Frost: ABC News)

He says the city's cool climate, close proximity to the federal government — a major client — and 100 per cent renewables-sourced electricity make it an ideal location.

"Canberra is great because it's actually quite cool and cold in winter," Mr Boorer said.

"But even during summer, it actually gets very pleasant in the evenings because of the altitude.

"So in a year-round sense, it's actually the coldest place in Australia that has all of the ingredients: so the energy, the power, the data connectivity and also the educated workforce that can actually make this industry very successful.

" A lot of the customers love to come to Canberra because immediately they understand that their facilities and their compute is actually powered by renewable energy out of the box. "

ACT data centres avoid community backlash seen overseas

With servers in a data centre generating a lot of heat, temperatures and stable power supply are key factors for operators.

CDC's data centre in Beard, which is still being fitted out, will have a total capacity of 40 megawatts (MW).

Compared to the entire ACT's highest recorded peak electricity demand last year of 732 MW — it is a lot of power.

The CDC Data Centres facility in the industrial suburb of Beard will have a total capacity of 40 MW when completed. (Harry Frost: ABC News)

Data centres also traditionally use tens of thousands of litres of water per year for cooling, which places increased pressure on local supplies.

Those demands on resources have — in part — prompted protests against data centres in parts of Australia and around the world.

But opposition to data centres in the ACT has been less vocal, which operators attribute to the use of "closed-loop" cooling systems that do not draw on the local water supply, as well as investment in renewable energy.

"I think a lot of the outrage is justified in a lot of parts of the world," Mr Boorer said.

He said many developments in the United States had not necessarily been in the right location, or operators had taken an "almost selfish approach".

"They're not thinking about how that generation could be leveraged across the grids for the benefit of the community more generally," he said.

"And so there hasn't been a lot of necessary benefit sharing from those types of developments."

The demands on energy and water supplies caused by data centres have prompted protests in communities around the world. (Supplied: Friends of the Earth)

Mr Boorer said the ACT had "a really consistent" set of planning laws and standards that the industry operated within.

"We have a national energy market, which is much more, I guess, sophisticated and mature and it's more sensibly arranged," he said.

"We match 100 per cent of our energy consumption with renewable energy today.

" Most people wouldn't even realise our facilities are here because we don't have a lot of the characteristics of the facilities that have not been wanted by the communities in other parts of the world. "

Barr says ACT already ahead of proposed national data centre rules

Last month the federal government announced future large-scale AI data centres could face mandatory requirements including minimising water use, underwriting new electricity generation and paying the full cost of connecting to the grid.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr says policy and practice around data centres in the ACT already aligns with the prime minister's intent for a new set of national standards and oversight for artificial intelligence.

Planning laws allow data centres in areas of the ACT zoned for industrial and services as well as broadacre sites outside urban areas — subject to planning rules and approvals processes.

Chief Minister Andrew Barr says data centres in the ACT already align with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese's intent for a new set of national standards. (ABC News)

"In the Australian context I think we sit at the ethical end of data centres and AI use, because it is principally around research institutions, government, national security and defence," Mr Barr said.

"Really the national scheme, if you like, would be catching up with where the ACT is at, not creating a new set of benchmarks that would exceed what we already do in the territory.

"It really is a best-in-class location for a certain type of data centre.

"But not the hyper-scale ones that have perhaps more commercial and beyond-government and security uses. They tend to go to larger and different markets, elsewhere in the world mostly."

Barr rejects pause on ACT data centre development

The federal government's proposal has prompted calls from community groups and the Greens for a moratorium on the development of large data centres until the rules are in place.

Mr Barr said the ACT government does not support a pause or halt to "responsible data centre development" while the national framework is being finalised.

"Data centres are currently assessed through the ACT's existing planning system in the same way as other developments," Mr Barr said.

"The ACT already has rigorous planning, environmental, utility and regulatory requirements and all development applications are considered on their individual merits and must comply with relevant planning, environmental and regulatory requirements."

There are already more than a dozen data centres in Canberra, including this NEXTDC one in Bruce. (ABC News: Matt Roberts)

Mr Boorer agrees the industry is likely to continue to expand in the ACT.

"I think Australia more generally is very attractive because of the political stability, the geopolitical kind of confidence that people have in Australia, the rule of law, the fact that we're a member of the Five Eyes Intelligence community," he said.

"They really do trust Australia and the Australian government — in any flavour to do the right thing and have high standards.

"We applaud the federal government actually taking control of the narrative around data centres and setting high standards because that will encourage the correct behaviour."

title: Program motivates remote students to join healthcare workforce at home
text:
In the remote Gulf town of Normanton, about 500 kilometres by road from Mount Isa, 17-year-old Melinda Burns grew up watching her aunt care for their community.

Her aunt spent 55 years working as a nurse with the North West Hospital and Health Service.

"Seeing my aunty give back to the community of Normanton, that is what I wanted to do," the teenager said.

Her aunt's name has been withheld for cultural reasons.

Melinda is one of seven Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander students who have completed Queensland Health's Deadly Start program in North West Queensland this year, its largest cohort since it launched locally in 2023.

Deadly Start is supporting First Nations students to gain qualifications and paid experience in health while completing high school. (Supplied: North West Hospital and Health Services)

All seven students who started the 2025–26 program have finished, giving the cohort a 100 per cent completion rate.

Across North West Queensland, where communities can be hundreds of kilometres from major health services, building a workforce that stays in the region is an ongoing challenge.

Deadly Start aims to address that by training young people who already call those communities home.

Indigenous workforce coordinator Shannon McConachie said people who trained locally were more likely to stay and work in regional and remote areas.

Shannon McConachie says training young people locally can help build a sustainable health workforce in the North West. (Supplied: North West Hospital and Health Services)

"We're investing in the young people who are already based in community and have strong ties to community," she said.

"It's a long-term solution, building a sustainable workforce from within our local communities."

Skills that can travel home

Deadly Start is a statewide school-based traineeship giving First Nations students paid, hands-on healthcare experience while they complete high school.

Students can work across maternity, allied health, medical wards and child and maternal health, while placements in Cloncurry and Normanton include hospital and aged care settings.

For students from remote communities including Normanton, Doomadgee and Mornington Island, the program can work around the distances they travel for school.

Those studying in Mount Isa can return to their home communities to complete placement hours during school holidays.

"By creating opportunities locally, young people can see a future for themselves in health right here in the North West," Ms McConachie said.

From school to patient care

Melinda first heard about Deadly Start during an information session at school.

She attends Gulf Christian College in Normanton and has spent one day each week undertaking a hospital placement, as well as completing additional hours during the Christmas holidays.

Her work has included helping patients with meals and bathing, changing beds and assisting nurses with general patient care.

The hands-on experience surprised her.

"There was a lot that I didn't think I would be able to do because I was only a trainee, but I did do quite a bit," she said.

Melinda Burns has achieved a Certificate III in health services assistance. (Supplied: North West Hospital Services)

Her family has also noticed a change in her confidence.

"A lot of my family say that they've seen me come out of my shell a lot more in terms of talking to people I've never met and just stepping out of my comfort zone," she said.

Trainees prepare for the workforce with a Certificate II in health support before moving on to a Certificate III in allied health, health service support and administration.

The students completed 375 hours, or 50 days, of paid employment as part of the vocational program.

Building the next generation

Three years after Deadly Start launched in the North West, the health service is seeing some of its earliest participants progress into further training and employment.

"We're starting to see some of the students through the first year that came through come back into our cadetship program, our tertiary program, and also come back into our leadership programs," Ms McConachie said.

Other former trainees have moved into aged care and youth services across the region.

For Melinda, the next step is back in Normanton.

After finishing school this year, she hopes to work at her local aged care facility or hospital, where a new renal unit is planned.

Caring for elders is particularly important to her.

"The elders, they're the base of the community," she said.

"They know a lot more about the land and all that than we would."

title: Meet the people working to tackle hate and foster social cohesion
text:
There was a notable shift in the tone of the antisemitism royal commission this week, as witnesses fronted the inquiry to highlight optimism about the grassroots work being done in the name of social cohesion.

Now entering its final week of public hearings, the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion has heard from academics, human rights specialists and community organisations about the importance of genuine human connection in combating division and hate in Australia.

The head of a unique childcare centre said it was important for this work to start with the very youngest of Australians before biases could form and take root.

Using a pseudonym, the Jewish Australian woman told the commission how her centre was teaching preschool children to look for familiar experiences and values in different cultures and traditions.

Each Friday, the centre participates in the Jewish tradition of challah baking, with the children making shapes in the dough and taking the fresh loaves home to be enjoyed with loved ones.

Challah baking is part of a Jewish tradition. (ABC News: Jane Cowan)

"There's this beautiful smell of the fresh bread and then it gets taken home in a little bag and it gets shared with their family," the woman said.

"It's a very distinct Jewish tradition … but the values underneath that is something that we all share. That idea of sharing food with family."

'The glue that connects us'

She said the model used by her centre was an example of a practical solution to tackling division.

"I wanted to note that over the course of these hearings, we've heard some of this harrowing evidence about antisemitism and really the complex challenges facing our society and at times it has been deeply confronting," she said.

"What I hope to offer today is something constructive. It's an opportunity to bring to the surface the shared human values that already connect us beneath our differences … it's the glue that connects us."

The two mates behind the compelling Brave Conversations initiative told the inquiry how they were working to equip university students with the skills to discuss uncomfortable topics safely.

Cognitive scientist Farid Zaid said the project was born from a need to help students distinguish between distress and discomfort.

Daniel Heller and Farid Zaid say they are teaching students to "stay in the room" when conversations get tough. (Supplied: Daniel Heller)

"I began just on my own introducing ways to help my students stay in the room when discomfort was presented to them, to show them that learning has to have an element of discomfort," he said.

" When disagreement is done well, it's a wonderful opportunity for connection, for learning, for growth, for innovation. "

Israeli and Palestinian historian Daniel Heller said the Brave Conversations workshops were always conducted in person and were not intended to be a "quick fix".

"So many of the issues that are plaguing Australian society involve tensions that are irreconcilable. They're never going to go away," he said.

"We try to shift the aim to be thinking about how we navigate tensions wisely together."

Opportunities for interfaith connection

Rabbi Zalman Kastel AM told the commission about the work the educational not-for-profit Together for Humanity was doing to create interfaith connections in schools.

"In our experience our success is very much driven by the fact that we are politically impartial, and we are inclusive and care about all communities," he said.

Rabbi Zalman Kastel is the founder of Together for Humanity. (Facebook: Together for Humanity)

"That resonates and moves young people very strongly when they can see, for example, a Muslim woman talking passionately about antisemitism or a Jewish rabbi talking about Islamophobia, or First Nations people talking about other people's prejudices."

The commission also heard there had been a chilling of some interfaith activities since the attack on Israel by terrorist organisation Hamas, and the subsequent war in Gaza.

Sandy Kouroupidis from the Faith Communities Council of Victoria said, historically, there had been regular interactions between Muslim and Jewish communities, including through school visits and exchanges.

"Unfortunately that doesn't exist anymore. A lot of the Jewish schools simply don't feel safe," he said.

'A very challenging space'

The inquiry heard from a number of cultural organisations, including the Australian United Solidarity for Iran, Rozanna Australia, Hindus Down Under and the Australian Multicultural Council.

Somali Society of NSW president Mohamed Hassan left Somalia at the age of 11 and is now involved in advocacy for his community while completing his second degree in law in Sydney.

Mohamed Hassan says community work can often be challenging. (ABC News: Greg Bigelow)

The 23-year-old said he spent his weekend going from event to event to develop relationships with different communities.

"It's a very challenging space. But every time before I go [to an event] I make sure that I understand the culture, religion and also the politics behind them," he said.

Mr Hassan said the way social cohesion was interpreted by communities and government could also be contentious.

"When social cohesion is presented primarily as a way of [getting] a particular community to integrate, adapt or change, they feel that they might be discriminated or they might be identified as the problem," he said.

'Wariness' around social cohesion

The issue came up again when the Australian Human Rights Commission's Giridharan Sivaraman told the inquiry some in the First Nations community were suspicious of work done in the name of social cohesion.

Giridharan Sivaraman says some view the notion of social cohesion with "wariness". (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

"In my consultations with the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander communities … there is a fundamental problem in that the notion of social cohesion doesn't reflect their particular position in our society, their need for self determination and sovereignty and their connection to this land," he said.

"That's where the concept of social cohesion is run counter to what it might be aiming to achieve, and I think its why many of the communities I engage with view the term with great wariness, and view any policy or plan associated with it with wariness.

"If we want to build a society where we live with equity, dignity and respect … then you actually have to do the hard work first of building racial literacy … and see diversity as a strength."

The royal commission will resume on Monday.

title: Five songs that show what the Brisbane music scene is made of
text:
Violent Soho's brand of beer-soaked, eardrum shattering alternative rock really has you feeling like you're listening to your favourite band underneath your mate's mum's house.

The Mansfield locals released one of the finest Australian rock albums this century with 2013's Hungry Ghost, including breakout single Covered in Chrome which landed at number 14 on the Hottest 100 that year.

Saramona Said flies under the radar, but deserves a shout-out based purely on its accompanying music video, directed by Brisbane filmmaker Dan Graetz and based on the renowned one-shot car scene from the 2006 film Children of Men.

"Mansfield's finest" Violent Soho took an indefinite hiatus in 2022, but reunited earlier this year. (Credit: Kane Hibberd)

Graetz's take is somewhat lighter in tone than the original, with four friends rolling through the streets of suburban Brisbane, before reaching a car park stage where the band blasts through the final chorus of the song for a raucous crowd.

"We're always a little bit behind Sydney and Melbourne, but at the same time, that gives Brisbane a chance to be something different, be itself," Graetz said.

" They really made where they came from, the whole Mansfield thing, a huge part of their identity, and the loyalty of their fans because of that was pretty incredible. "

The video's final moments will feel familiar to anyone who's caught Violent Soho live — they're some of the most high energy gigs out there.

And the rest of the video will feel familiar to anyone who spent their 20s picking up mates after work or uni to head out and find trouble.

"The idea was being in the world of these fans of the band rather than the band itself and how it feels to go to a gig … it was more about just the excitement of getting to it and then what it feels like to run into the back of a mosh pit," Graetz said.

title: Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two
text:

SportCricketTest cricket Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two Nick Wright August 23, 2026 — 11:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Mackay: Australia will look to level the two-Test series with Bangladesh as early as Sunday, after a slice of Bangladeshi history ended the hosts’ first innings in the first session of day two with a commanding 146-run lead. It took a toe-crushing yorker from Shoriful Islam to end Cameron Green’s valiant lone hand with the bat, trapped in front on 67 as the left-arm seam bowler became Bangladesh’s first quick to claim seven wickets in a Test innings (7-48). Cameron Green was out leg before wicket in Australia’s first innings. Getty Images That milestone followed his nation’s first Test win on Australian soil in the first clash in Darwin. Green had looked composed throughout his innings until receiving the Shoriful peach, playing fluently until stumps on day one as wickets fell around him during a dramatic collapse of 5-30 from Steve Smith’s dismissal for 42.

Advertisement

The 27-year-old all-rounder appeared on track to back up his second innings 104 in the first Test in Darwin with a fourth career ton, playing one powerful cut shot and another elegant off-drive for boundaries inside the first three overs of day two at Great Barrier Reef Arena. When Green fell, Nathan Lyon ensured Australia moved beyond 200 – a well-timed on drive to the fence, and pull shot over it, featuring in his unbeaten 32 before Josh Hazlewood was out caught for six attempting to take on spinner Taijul Islam, ending Australia’s stand at 210. Bangladesh bowler Shoriful Islam celebrates his seven-wicket haul against Australia. Getty Images But Bangladesh were in early disarray when they came out to bat for the second time. While there were no repeats of Starc’s first-ball scalp on day one, Tanzid Hasan driving him down the ground to the boundary, the veteran quick did cause carnage in his second over. First, he caught Shadman Islam high on the bat with a sharp, straightening delivery, with Marnus Labuschagne diving forward from point for the catch. Next ball, the left-arm spearhead was on a hat-trick for the second time this Test, as Mominul Haque shouldered arms to a ball that nipped back and knocked out his off stump, to leave Bangladesh reeling at 2-5.

Advertisement

There were 18 wickets to fall on day one, Starc setting the tone by sealing his five-wicket haul after just 43-minutes, finishing with figures of 6-12 as the visitors struggled to contend with the extra bounce and lively green pitch. Despite the carnage, Starc said he had no issues with the pitch on Saturday. “People will sit there and go ’18 wickets, it’s a bad wicket’. I think it’s a very good day one wicket, I think it’s probably played very similar to a Gabba wicket – you see a little bit of tennis ball bounce early at the Gabba, and likewise today,” Starc said. “It was a pretty helter-skelter day of cricket, but I’d say some good bowling led to 18 wickets, as opposed to the wicket.” Should Starc and his fellow quicks roll Bangladesh in similar fashion, there will be no further chances for Labuschagne, Beau Webster and Matt Renshaw to push their case for inclusion in the forthcoming series in South Africa.

While Renshaw (eight) would be expected to be given a reprieve, having only just been brought into the side to replace axed opener Jake Weatherald, both Labuschagne and Webster have struggled for a more prolonged period. Webster, to his credit, had not put a foot wrong in his career until this two-Test series. However, he has managed just 17 runs across three knocks – including a first innings duck in Mackay. Labuschagne’s long-term struggles, meanwhile, have been well-documented – failing to score a century since July 2023, while averaging just 29.69 since the start of that year following his cheap dismissal for four on Saturday.

title: They rejected the Aussie dream. What they bought instead cost $130,000
text:
A sprawling property with a white picket fence was once a symbol of success, but for Lizzie Villestas this version of home ownership is a trap, not a triumph.

"For many, success is measured by the square footage of your property and for us, we began to see large homes as a different kind of trap; one that comes with massive debt and endless maintenance," Villestas told SBS Chinese.

For more than three years, she has lived in a tiny house measuring just eight metres long and 2.5 metres wide, or 20 square metres. The average floor area of a new house in Australia was 232.3 square metres in 2021/22, according to the Australian Bureau of Statistics.

Villestas' space may be small, but it's been thoughtfully designed, featuring a deep green and timber colour palette, akin to the surrounding bushland. It's even fitted with a study loft, bathtub and an indoor fireplace.

A labour of love, the property was constructed by Villestas and David Menhennett over 18 months and cost about $130,000. The couple now live in north-east Victoria and can relocate their tiny house on wheels across Australia, as desired.

News that makes sense Your trusted source for staying up-to-date with the world around you. Get free daily news updates and analysis, straight to your inbox. Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"It was a virtual no-brainer ... most Australians are looking down the barrel of now ... a 30-year mortgage of up to a million dollars to own an average home," said Menhennett, who previously lived in Hong Kong for around 20 years.

Compounded by Australia's housing crisis, experts believe demand for tiny houses is surging. But while these properties promise big savings, they're often associated with regulatory red tape and financing complexities.

A dwelling, a vehicle or both?

Driven by a desire to achieve financial freedom, Danielle Lester decided to adopt tiny house living two years ago.

She now serves as president of the volunteer-run Australian Tiny Homes Association (ATHA) but admits it's difficult to gather robust data about the number of tiny homes in Australia.

"Our membership base doesn't fully represent the amount of people who are living in tiny homes around Australia, and we find because of the regulatory complexity, a lot of people are choosing to do it under the radar, at their own risk," Lester told SBS News.

"Obviously, people have got no other option at the moment but to find a roof to put over their heads."

In part, that's because there's no official national definition for what constitutes a tiny house in Australia. Instead, they are regulated by federal, state and local government authorities — whose planning policies can often overlap and contradict each other.

Griffith University emeritus professor Paul Burton said tiny homes are also classified differently depending on their design.

That includes tiny houses fixed to the ground, which is "like a conventional house only smaller".

Burton told SBS News the image that usually comes to mind when people think of these properties is a tiny house on wheels:

"So, that's something that can be hitched to a truck or car and moved a bit like a caravan. They are treated under a lot of legislation or local laws passed by councils ... like a caravan, even though they're not really the same."

The tiny houses market in Australia has evolved to offer affordable, mid-tier and high end designs to cater to the growing clientele. Credit: Lizzie Villestas and David Menhennett

In NSW, one caravan can legally be installed on a property without council approval if it is connected with and occupied by members of the owner's household.

If a person is staying longer-term on land they do not own, they typically need council approval. In NSW, this usually involves submitting a development application and, in some cases, engineering certificates about the structural safety of a tiny home on wheels.

In June, Shellharbour City Council on the south coast of NSW announced it would take a different approach. It has adopted a two-year trial program which removes the need for a development application for tiny houses used as rental accommodation.

In 2025, Bega Valley Shire Council — also in NSW — issued a compliance order asking that a tiny house on wheels it deemed unauthorised be demolished. Owners of the tiny house have since lodged an appeal through the NSW Land and Environment Court.

Burton believes local council approaches are "inconsistent" and said ATHA is working on a national advocacy strategy to "help unpack the complexity of the tiny house world".

Financing for tiny houses

Jamie Mitchell is a senior broker at Great Escape Finance and told SBS News that because tiny houses on wheels are not classified as dwellings, they are not eligible for home loans.

He said another "hurdle" is that not all tiny houses follow the same construction codes, so for a long time lenders wouldn't take security over the property.

"There's no guarantee that the person who built the tiny home has done a good job. So, there are definitely builders that have been around and now have a good reputation. But from a lender's point of view, they're still quite risk-averse."

Mitchell said his company now works with several personal and commercial loan lenders to enable financing for tiny houses. Generally, the maximum loan term for a personal loan is up to seven years.

Last year, Commonwealth Bank also announced it would become the first major bank to offer a construction loan for prefabricated houses.

When asked whether demand for tiny house financing has grown in recent years, Mitchell laughed and admitted, "I'm just so swamped at the moment, it's just ridiculous."

"To give you an idea, our record for the amount of turnover that we did in a month historically, in March this year we more than doubled that ... and every month since has been pretty close to what that original record was."

Mitchell's clients were typically single women "that might have been divorced and were heading towards retirement". Now, the demographic has shifted to include more young families and single professionals planning to live permanently in tiny houses.

A risky investment?

According to the ATHA, a professionally built tiny house on wheels can cost between $80,000 and more than $170,000 depending on the size, design and customisation of the property.

But unlike traditional houses, which tend to increase in value after purchase, Burton cautioned that tiny houses on wheels can depreciate over time.

"When we talk about increasing house prices, what's typically increasing is the land value, not the structure itself ... so, a tiny house on wheels unless it's very special ... it's probably going to diminish or at best hold its value."

Lester believes the amount she is paying to rent land for her tiny house is significantly cheaper than rental accommodation she has experienced in the past.

"Not only that, I've got full control over my environment, my living situations, my surroundings," she said.

Like a caravan, a tiny house on wheels can be relocated as required. Credit: Lizzie Villestas and David Menhennett

"This cost of living crisis affects everybody, landlords included, which can have knock-on effects on their ability to maintain your property in an adequate way. So, I think savings to be had from living in a tiny house and renting land are significant."

For Villestas, who previously lived in Hong Kong in a small apartment, tiny living is not just a cost-saving measure, but a lifestyle choice.

"There is a growing community that is going towards this alternative living because of the pressures that the housing crisis is causing at the moment. It just gives the future generations a little bit of hope, to be able to own ... buy and own a property.

"You've just got to have an open mind if you want to live the way that we live, but it is certainly possible."

title: 'Obesity paradox': Study finds common health metric could be misleading for older people
text:
Key Points A "normal" BMI does not necessarily indicate low health risk, particularly when accompanied by a larger waist circumference, researchers say.

Rather than using BMI alone, they suggest considering waist circumference, muscle mass, body composition and a person's overall health.

A person's Body Mass Index (BMI) may not tell the full story about their risk of dying in older age, with new research suggesting waist circumference can identify risks that a normal BMI misses.

The study of 6,905 adults in the United States aged 65 and over found that being overweight was associated with a lower mortality hazard than having a normal BMI, particularly among men.

But a larger waist circumference was associated with a higher mortality hazard in both men and women.

The researchers say the findings do not mean obesity is protective. Instead, they highlight the limitations of using BMI as the sole indicator of a person's health.

BMI, or body mass index, is a measure calculated from a person's height and weight. It is commonly used to classify people as underweight, normal weight, overweight or obese, but it does not distinguish between muscle and fat.
