Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

"BMI and waist circumference provide complementary information about health risk in older adults," co-author Dr Bryan Blissmer from the University of Rhode Island said.

"Our findings suggest that considering both measures together, rather than relying on BMI alone, may improve mortality risk assessment and support more informed clinical decision-making."

What did the study consider?

In the study, a BMI below 18.5 was considered underweight, 18.5 to 24.9 was considered normal weight, 25 to 29.9 was considered overweight, and 30 or above was considered obese.

Obesity was divided into three classes: Class I, BMI 30 to 34.9; Class II, 35 to 39.9; and Class III, 40 or above.

However, for their analysis, the researchers combined Class I and Class II into a single category.

The researchers analysed 14 years of data from the US National Health and Aging Trends Study, following 6,905 people from 2011 to 2024.

They used a statistical measure called a hazard ratio to compare the likelihood of death occurring over the follow-up period between different groups.

A hazard ratio of 1 indicates no difference from the comparison group. A value below 1 indicates a lower hazard of death, while a value above 1 indicates a higher hazard.

For example, a hazard ratio of 0.5 represents roughly half the mortality hazard of the comparison group, while a ratio of 2 represents roughly twice the hazard.

What were the results for men and women?

The study found important differences between men and women, particularly in the relationship between BMI and mortality.

Among men, being overweight was associated with a 46 per cent lower mortality hazard than having a normal BMI. Men with Class I or II obesity also had a lower mortality hazard, at 51 per cent lower than men in the normal BMI range.

The pattern was weaker among women. Overweight women had a 27 per cent lower mortality hazard than women with a normal BMI. The lower hazard observed among women with Class I or II obesity was not statistically significant, suggesting it may have been due to chance.

READ MORE Can this small patch really help you lose weight and live a healthier life?

Waist circumference showed a much more consistent pattern. A waist circumference above 40 inches (102 centimetres) for men or 35 inches (89 centimetres) for women was associated with a 24 per cent higher mortality hazard in both sexes, independent of BMI.

The researchers also found that a normal BMI could mask higher risk. Men with a normal BMI but a high waist circumference had a 33 per cent higher mortality hazard, while women had a 23 per cent higher hazard.

Being underweight was also associated with almost twice the mortality hazard in both men and women.

Overall, the association between higher BMI and lower mortality was stronger in men, whereas the relationship between larger waist circumference and higher mortality was similar in both sexes.

Understanding the 'obesity paradox'

Associate professor David Scott from Deakin University's Institute for Physical Activity said that measuring health solely by BMI creates an "obesity paradox".

"It demonstrates the 'obesity paradox': the finding that in older adults and some populations with chronic health conditions, higher body mass indexes, even in the overweight or obese range, can protect against mortality," he said.

BMI cannot distinguish between muscle and fat, nor can it show where fat is stored.

"Because BMI does not distinguish between fat and lean mass, the 'obesity paradox' may be explained by the fact that some people classified as overweight or obese have high amounts of lean mass and relatively low amounts of fat mass, while others who appear to be a healthy weight may actually have a high body fat percentage," Scott added.

The researchers argue that waist circumference can provide important additional information because fat stored around the abdomen is associated with metabolic and cardiovascular problems.

The researchers say the findings support a broader approach to assessing health in older adults.

Rather than relying on BMI alone, they suggest considering waist circumference, muscle mass, body composition and a person's overall health.

For older adults, the study's central message is that a "normal" or "healthy" BMI does not necessarily indicate low health risk, particularly when accompanied by a larger waist circumference.

title: Can Australia rebuild social cohesion? Inquiry hears calls for change
text:
in brief Over four days, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about social cohesion and antisemitism.

The commission is in its 9th and final block of hearings.

Experts, advocates and community leaders are calling for stronger social cohesion and action on antisemitism, telling an inquiry "we need to break the cycle".

Over four days of hearings this week, commissioner Virginia Bell heard concerns about declining satisfaction with democracy, social media polarisation, racism, self-censorship and the breakdown of relationships between religious and cultural communities.

The Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion also heard proposals for stronger education about Jewish Australians, better recognition of migrants’ qualifications and more effective approaches to tackling prejudice.

But the hearings also exposed difficult questions about what social cohesion should mean, including how Australia can combat discrimination without silencing debate.

The royal commission, launched in response to the December 2025 Bondi terror attack, is in its ninth and final block of hearings, with its final report due in December.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

Here are the key takeaways from the week.

Questions about democracy

Professors Nicholas Biddle and Matthew Gray, both from the Australian National University, fronted the royal commission on Monday, speaking to reporters about democratic attitudes in Australia and responses about declining satisfaction with democracy.

Their June report found that satisfaction with democracy fell to its lowest level since January 2023, while principled support for democracy increased. Professor Gray said multiple factors could be at play, including social media undermining support for democracy.

"We conclude that efforts to counter antisemitism will be limited unless they also address the platforms through which distrust, polarisation and extremist narratives circulate," Gray told the commission.

He argued targeted interventions, particularly for young Australians with low educational attainment and low levels of principled democratic support, would be more effective than universal attempts to counter antisemitism.

"Because trust in core institutions is closely associated with democratic commitment, consideration should be given to how government agencies, education systems and public communications practices could be made more transparent, accountable and credible, particularly in communities experiencing disadvantage," Gray said.

Ahmed Hegazi, a strategic adviser, and his friend Joel Lazar, the chief executive of the Jewish Climate Network, also expressed concern about polarisation and emphasised the importance of cross-cultural communication.

"Humans who know their neighbours don't feel they are threats and they don't fear them, they feel connected to them," Hegazi said. "We need to break the cycle."

"There's basically no alternative to trying new things even if they're hard … as fathers of young children, we know important things are always hard," Lazar said.

Skills recognition proposed to ease tensions

Australian businessman, David Gonski told the inquiry his 24-member Antisemitism Education Taskforce was considering a proposal to improve recognition of migrants' skills and address community tensions.

Many skilled migrants were underemployed because their previous qualifications were not recognised.

"This, (a member) put to us, creates some tension and concern both within them and the people that they live with, and so on," he said on Tuesday.

"He felt that we could find a twofold solution: a solution that allowed us to have more skilled workers, and ... that would take away some of the aggravation that comes for these people."

Gonski said "there was merit" in considering the proposal but the task force had not reached a final decision. He stressed he was not suggesting further migration, but broader permissions for migrants to practice in their fields.

Gonski was appointed to lead the antisemitism education task force in December 2025 and previously filed the Gonski report on Australian education funding.

He also recommended broader education about Jewish contributions to Australia.

"We are hopeful that (the Australian Curriculum, Assessment and Reporting Authority) will now look more broadly at not just Holocaust studies, but also more generally the contribution of the Jews and indeed the Jewish faith," he said.

"There's a lot of contribution by Jews to Australia, to the history of Australia."

Orthodox Rabbi Zalman Kastel suggested educators address specific prejudices in youth's education.

"Telling people a general message of don't be racist, doesn't cut it," he said.

Monash University lecturers Farid Zaid and Daniel Heller said students and staff had become afraid to address difficult topics, with many students struggling to hear different views.

"We both saw conversations in the classroom play out along really rigid lines," Zaid said.

"I was deeply surprised by my students' inability to distinguish discomfort in the classroom ... and distressed."

Most students and academics adopted self-censorship for fear of social media censure or official complaints. Others were inclined to, in Said and Heller's terms, "perform certainty"; project a sense of virtue over others.

"We know what's virtuous, what's moral, what's right; and anyone who disagrees is, in one way or another, morally reprehensible," Heller said.

The pair run Brave Conversations Project workshops teaching students and teachers how to stay in the room when discussions become difficult.

Terror attacks deepen Jewish-Muslim division

Faith Communities Council of Victoria's Sandy Kouroupidis said interaction between Jewish and Muslim communities had stopped altogether following the Bondi massacre on 14 December 2025, and the attack on Israel by Hamas militants on 7 October 2023.

The October 7 attacks by Hamas killed 1,200 people and resulted in 250 people being taken hostage, according to Israeli tallies. Israel's subsequent military campaign in Gaza has killed more than 70,000 people and been labeled a genocide by a United Nations commission, which the Israeli government disputes.

READ MORE Australia facing unprecedented levels of online hate speech, antisemitism inquiry told

"We have two vice chairs; one of them is the chair of the Islamic Council of Victoria and the other one is the chair of the Jewish Community Council of Victoria," he said.

"It has been very, very challenging to get those two communities in the same room."

Jewish people had stopped attending interfaith events, while schools stopped visiting Muslim and Christian institutes.

"A lot of the Jewish schools simply don't feel safe," he said.

Social cohesion must not hide racism

Race Discrimination Commissioner Giridharan Sivaraman warned that social cohesion can camouflage racial discrimination.

"Stop talking about racism because you're disrupting the social cohesion," Sivaraman said he was told by a senior government official.

He said social cohesion policies could resemble those used to justify racial assimilation and cause distrust.

"If it's obscuring, then it's not actually solving the systemic or structural problem that you need to fix," he told the inquiry.

"If your experience of policies or laws or programs under the term social cohesion are ones where you're excluded ... or you have to assimilate ... you won't trust the institutions you're engaging with."

Mourners place flowers at a memorial at Bondi Beach in Sydney, Saturday, December 20, 2025. Australia is in mourning after gunmen opened fire on Bondi Beach, killing 15 people in an attack designed to target the Jewish community. (AAP Image/Bianca De Marchi) NO ARCHIVING Source: AAP / Bianca De Marchi

Sivaraman also said reports of antisemitism, particularly in workplaces, had risen sharply since the October 7 attacks on Israel.

"Workplaces ended up being a really consistent theme that came up as an area where people felt disadvantaged," Sivaraman said.

"(They felt) they couldn't express their identity, felt they were in danger of losing their job, felt the inquiry also heard conflicting views over where legitimate criticism of Zionism ends and antisemitism begins."

READ MORE Five key takeaways from the first week of antisemitism royal commission hearings

Separately, Rita Jabri Markwell, principal policy adviser to the Australian Muslim Advocacy Network, argued Zionism should be treated as a political ideology rather than a protected characteristic.

"It's not a race or religion," she said.

Jewish witnesses had described Zionism as inseparable from their religious and cultural identity. Markwell argued courts had increasingly taken her view and warned that treating Zionism as protected risked excluding Jewish Australians who rejected the ideology.

"The mere fact that there is a portion of Jewish people who do not accept that it is central to their identity indicates that it is an ideology," she said.

— With additional reporting from AAP

title: This Liberal MP took a journey from northern China — heading somewhere few Australians dare visit
text:
Ted O'Brien's path to Parliament has taken him where few Australians, and indeed Westerners, have gone before: North Korea’s capital, Pyongyang.

Before becoming an MP, the Opposition foreign affairs spokesperson worked across Asia.

He was living in Beijing with his wife Sophia, who was working for the International Crisis Group, when the opportunity came to join a small group of fifteen to visit the authoritarian state in 2010.

The occasion was the 65th anniversary of the ruling Workers' Party — at a time when Kim Jong-il’s reign was waning, and the transition was underway to son Kim Jong-Un.

"The North Koreans choreographed everything, but you can't hide everything," he told SBS News.

He spent most of the visit in the North Korean capital, arriving by air and leaving by train through northern China.

The Australian government now lists North Korea in the "do not travel" category on its official Smartraveller advice portal.

The access O'Brien had to the secretive nation is rare.

"You'd hop in a bus, you'd go to a school and you'd meet a few parents and school kids. Then you'd go to a small shopping strip, and you'd realise the kids from the school, the same kids at the shopping strip."

Ted O'Brien visited North Korea with a small group of fifteen in 2010. Source: SBS News / Supplied

"It'd be like this theatre that would follow us around trying to portray a very different North Korea."

One encounter with reality came, perhaps ironically, at the sprawling Kumsusan Palace of the Sun, where the state’s leaders are buried, and it serves as the sacred centre of the North Korean mythos.

O’Brien says the "organisers muddled things up" and his tour ended up sharing a room with a group of workers, the best in each of their factories, given the coveted opportunity to pay their respects.

"This was the moment of their life … wearing their best possible, albeit all the same uniform," O'Brien recounts.

READ MORE Trump and Kim's renewed bromance stirs new and old threats for Australia

"That is where you saw their real poverty, and it sounds crude to say it, but you could smell the poverty, you could see the poverty, the eyes completely focusing down.

"And this is people's most happy day in their life. That will always stay with me of just a human reminder of what an authoritarian regime can mean."

After working across Asia, including Taiwan and China, O’Brien was elected to the seat of Fairfax in 2016, and now the Coalition's foreign affairs spokesperson has been putting his "rusty" Mandarin skills to use, fronting Liberal Party messaging on Chinese language social media, and giving speeches in the language.

"I'm a big believer that there's nothing more important than national unity," he explains.

"I think national unity is a critical part of our national security. It is vitally important if we are to withstand coercion as a country.”

While describing English as Australia’s "primary language”, O'Brien says politicians also need to "respect the dignity of the individual”, claiming English as a "far harder" language to learn than Chinese.

"If an individual is still struggling to engage with our national language, well, let me engage with him or her in their language if we can, so they understand that once they become an Australian, they are absolutely part of our family as Aussies.”

The last Liberal Party review was scathing about the party’s struggles to engage with multicultural communities, identifying "the party's capacity to thoughtlessly offend groups, including the Chinese" as a "widespread problem", and singling out how Jane Hume’s remarks about "Chinese spies" were successfully weaponised by Labor in the final days of the campaign.

O’Brien argued his in-language approach was driven by a "genuine desire to ensure we have unity in Australia", saying he’s picked up on concerns among Chinese Australian voters about Beijing's ethnic unity laws.

"They need to know that their country is absolutely with them, that there's nothing more important than being an Australian."

Separately, O'Brien was partially successful in pressuring the government to amend updated foreign arrangements laws to force greater scrutiny of academics' independent research.

The Coalition had voiced concerns that a loophole in the laws allowed researchers to independently collaborate with institutions from so-called "rogue" states, without Commonwealth oversight.

"If it falls under the auspices of a university, then the Commonwealth knows about it. But if the professor decides to do it on his own without the university banner, the Commonwealth doesn't know about it. The risk is the same to the Australian people," he said.

This week, Foreign Minister Penny Wong intervened to shut down an ANU partnership with China’s Shandong University by 2027. It followed a Pentagon call to blacklist the institution over concerns about its research links with the Chinese state.

"What we have to have is risk-aware engagement; that's the approach we've taken, that's the approach we need," Wong said.

title: Trump pledged support for fossil fuels. Now his war in Iran is fast-tracking renewables
text:
Donald Trump had a busy February.

On 11 February, the United States president signed an executive order directing the military and the Pentagon — already emitting carbon dioxide at volumes comparable to the Philippines — to source their energy from coal.

For that, the CEO of the country's largest coal company awarded him a bronze trophy, declaring him the "undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal".

A day later, Trump and Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) administrator Lee Zeldin repealed the foundational 2009 greenhouse gas endangerment finding, stripping the EPA of its authority to regulate carbon dioxide and methane emissions.

Then, on 14 February, he established the National Energy Dominance Council, a federal body designed to fast-track oil, gas and coal projects at minimal cost and without environmental impact assessment — fulfilling his election promise to "drill, baby, drill".

Two weeks later, the US was firing missiles at Iran.

The retaliatory Iranian blockade of the Strait of Hormuz and attacks on Gulf state infrastructure have created an energy crisis the likes of which the world has never seen.

Oil and gas disruptions are expected to continue for months, even years.

Peabody Energy CEO James Grech (left) presented a bronze statue of a coal miner to Donald Trump on 11 February. Source: Getty / Anna Moneymaker

At the same time, the world is warming at its fastest rate in geological history, driven by the burning of those same fossil fuels.

The transition away from them has not been happening fast enough to avoid the kind of warming that exacerbates extreme weather events, such as the recent catastrophic wildfires in Europe and North America or the "exceptionally unusual" El Niño event presently brewing.

For many countries, the cost of switching away from fossil fuels has outweighed the urgency of the climate crisis, slowing the transition to renewable energy.

But that appears to be changing. Trump's decision to engage Iran in a protracted military conflict has prompted a global rethink of traditional energy sources — inadvertently strengthening the case for investment in renewables at a time when market conditions are increasingly favourable.

Some experts suggest it could be the inflection point needed to bend climate projections in a more survivable direction — but it has also prompted a major doubling down in some areas, which could have the opposite effect.

Economic drivers trump environmental urgency

Since the war broke out at the end of February, at least 29 countries have enacted structural policy decisions to decarbonise their economies, the International Energy Agency (IEA) reports.

Australia is among them, having announced an expansion of public EV charging stations, funding to electrify the Australia Post fleet and a zero-emission heavy freight transport project.

Overseas, the European Union has fast-tracked a mandate requiring solar panels to be installed on all new buildings by the end of the year; France and Germany have redirected billions from fossil fuel subsidies into heat-pump grants; India has commissioned 500 new biogas plants (which convert organic waste into renewable energy and nutrient-rich fertiliser); while New Delhi and Mumbai have switched all new public buses to electric.

Even in the US, a major high-voltage transmission project has been fast-tracked to deliver Canadian hydropower to New York and New England.

Experts say such emergency policy measures are being driven by economic needs in the wake of the crisis, the third this decade to rocket global fuel prices, following the COVID-19 pandemic and Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine.

The current situation, however, is accelerating fossil fuel "demand destruction" on a larger scale, independent climate analyst Ketan Joshi says.

"Those previous crises did not occur when there was a cheap, readily available alternative to both oil consumption and gas consumption," Joshi tells SBS News.

The policy response also signals the growing importance of domestic power generation, according to Roc Shi, professor of energy, environmental economics and sustainability at the University of Technology Sydney.

READ MORE The lessons from the Middle East war Australia can't afford to ignore

He believes the present crisis "will impact any future assessment scenario for governments".

"The crisis makes people realise that relying on the global supply of oil and energy actually [makes them] vulnerable to the new reality. That will undermine and damage the comparative advantages of fossil fuels," Shi says.

A global 'turning point'

That economic rationale is already driving major renewable projects worldwide, especially in parts of Asia that have historically depended on oil and gas imports for energy production.

In South Korea, there is a huge push to ensure commercial truck and shipping infrastructure will soon run on hydrogen.

In Vietnam, the country's largest conglomerate Vingroup recently announced a major hybrid renewable and battery storage project, replacing its previous proposal to build the country's largest liquefied natural gas (LNG) import terminal and power plant.

In China, now the world's biggest producer of green energy, the rapid uptake of renewables has been fuelled in part by energy security concerns, along with the economic growth potential of green technology and manufacturing. In the first six months of this year, more than 40 per cent of its electricity came from renewables, according to China’s National Energy Administration.

Sofia Gonzales-Zuñiga, a senior climate policy analyst with Climate Analytics, tells SBS News the crisis has been a wake-up call for many countries. Those that have been sluggish to act on environmental grounds are now seeing the economic appeal.

"Things are changing very fast now," she says.

You have mature technology that is price-competitive and that can be easily scalable.

Over the past decade, renewable energy installation costs have fallen dramatically, opening up market opportunities in regions that previously saw the transition as cost-prohibitive.

According to research from Our World in Data, solar photovoltaic costs fell by 90 per cent over the decade to 2024, onshore wind costs dropped by 70 per cent, and battery costs by more than 90 per cent.

As costs have dropped, capacity has grown. And with an energy crisis once again inflating fuel prices, conditions are ripe for long-term change, Gonzales-Zuñiga says.

"The expectation is that this could be that turning point where afterwards there's no return to fossil fuels."

The 'solar revolution'

Pakistan's response to the 2022 energy crisis offers a domestic example.

Following Russia's invasion of Ukraine, international sanctions halted the supply of Russian oil to Europe. In response, contractors re-routed shipments, chasing enlarged profits in Europe, which sent global fuel prices soaring.

At the time, Pakistan was generating 25 per cent of its power from LNG imported via Qatar. The country suffered devastating rolling blackouts as a result of the price hikes and quickly began seeking alternatives.

Haneea Isaad, a Pakistan-based energy finance specialist at the Institute for Energy Economics and Financial Analysis (IEEFA), says solar energy was the obvious choice.

A man washing solar panels during a heat wave in Jacobabad, Pakistan, in 2022. Source: Getty / Bloomberg

China was producing a "massive surplus" of solar panels for relatively low cost at the time, she explains. In addition, the newly elected government in Pakistan slashed taxes and import charges on them, while implementing "generous" energy buyback schemes.

"Anybody who could really afford to put up a rooftop solar system went for it," Isaad says.

Pakistan quickly became the world's largest importer of solar panels. Over the next two years, almost 30 gigawatts of solar energy was installed; rural areas were electrified for the first time and demand for coal, oil and LNG dropped.

Joshua Runciman, lead Australian gas analyst at IEEFA, describes it as a "human-led solar revolution".

"It potentially serves as an example of the way that individuals — not energy planners, not wonks in ivory towers — but individuals might actually respond to [the current crisis]," he says.

Thanks to Pakistan's solar revolution, when gas stopped flowing through the Strait of Hormuz in March — essentially cutting off all LNG supplies from Qatar — the country was better positioned to respond than it was in 2022.

Waqas Moosa, head of solar energy company Hedron Solar in Pakistan, says other countries can learn from Pakistan.

"Malaysia, Philippines, India, Bangladesh, they suffered," he says, referring to the fallout of the crisis ignited by Trump's war on Iran.

The sun does not pass through the Strait of Hormuz or any other strait or chokepoint which is going to come in the future.

With solar panel sales rising dramatically over the last few years — which Moosa notes coincided with prices falling — he expects to see similar revolutions around the world as countries enter "the renewable era".

"The Stone Age did not end because stone finished, the Iron Age did not end because iron finished, and the fossil fuel age is not going to end because we ran out of fossil fuel," he says.

"Maybe 30, 40 years down the road, when the kids study history, they'll probably look at this decade, the 2020s, where the transition from fossil fuels towards renewables happened."

Billions and billions of dollars

Even as rapid change is underway in some parts of the world, the status quo prevails in others.

Research from Climate Analytics shows that nearly one-third of the global population lives in a country that is highly economically dependent on fossil fuel exports.

So while many importing nations have hastened their transition to renewables since Trump authorised the first strikes on Iran in February, some exporting nations have sought to capitalise on increased global demand for fuel.

US exports of LNG have surged to an all-time high while Canada has enacted emergency legislation to fast-track new mining and export projects, simultaneously reneging on its global climate pledges.

Other countries without established renewable resources have also increased their use of coal for power generation, including Japan, Bangladesh, Thailand and the Philippines.

Even China, increasingly touted as a green energy leader, has walked back coal-reduction commitments, choosing instead to focus on building its renewable-led power sector, underpinned by coal.

Indeed, the country remains the world's biggest carbon emitter. Its domestic coal-fired power generation is expected to rise by 1.5 to 3 per cent this year, reversing last year's first-in-a-decade decline.

Globally, coal use is predicted to increase 1.4 per cent.

Across the world, politicians have used the crisis to argue for slowing or reversing the energy transition on economic or energy security grounds, something Joshi says is "very convincing".

In Australia, Opposition leader Angus Taylor has said "we must dig and we must drill" in response to the current global shock. The Liberal Party and One Nation have both promised to abandon net zero frameworks entirely, arguing they hamper energy security.

Such favourable political backing gives fossil fuel companies greater licence to continue generating already vastly inflated profits.

Analytics firm Wood Mackenzie estimates the global oil and gas industry is on track for a nearly $700 billion cash windfall this year. When oil peaked at US$126 a barrel in April, the world's top 100 oil companies were making a combined US$30 million ($43 million) in profit every hour.

"This money just becomes a war chest," Joshi says.

"They can use it for political lobbying, for communications, to build new fossil fuel infrastructure. I think we can say confidently that it makes them more capable in enacting their agenda."

'The last push for fossil fuels'

The tug-of-war between renewables and fossil fuels is affecting global emissions in real-time, too.

While the IEA predicted at the beginning of the year that emissions would finally begin to drop, the onset of war in Iran saw carbon emissions spike sharply. It represents a departure from other recent energy crises, which have typically triggered a temporary drop in emissions.

Source: SBS News

The IEA now expects emissions to rise to a new record once again this year.

Gonzales-Zuñiga says a "lot is changing in the background"; however, political resistance and entrenched interests continue to offset meaningful climate action.

"There's this last push for fossil fuels, like, the last dying push," she says.

I think we are exactly at that threshold where it just needs to go in the other direction.

If the world could rally to implement the Global Stocktake goals agreed to at COP28 — tripling renewable capacity, doubling energy efficiency, and cutting methane — by 2030, it would reduce projected warming by 0.9 degrees this century.

"If this crisis were to tip the scales in that direction, this could be like a reference point for how far we could go," Gonzales-Zuñiga says.

With economic factors, not environmental ones, driving the rollout of renewable energy so far, it's not yet clear whether uptake will moderate long-term projections beyond the war.

Joshi says the simultaneous push for renewables and the doubling down on fossil fuels seem to be having a "counter-balancing" effect, with no clear overall direction.

"If I had to guess, electrification in Asia and a general nervousness around fossil fuel use will result in a material reduction in fossil fuels, but not necessarily enough to make that curve plummet downwards — you know, like it should have 10 years ago."

He adds that a renewables transition powered by concern over energy security is also unsustainable, as once that issue is resolved, "the impetus to switch away from fossil fuels just drops".

"It probably does have some side benefits for climate, but in general, it is just not a great way of enacting this change."

If you could design a perfect world, you would opt for a much better way of doing things.

With the war in Iran now in its sixth month and fuel prices again climbing, some experts are sceptical about whether the crisis will amount to lasting change.

And yet, undeniably, it has also hastened the fast-tracking of renewable projects in some regions which otherwise may not have happened — including in the US.

In Texas, America's most oil-rich, deep-red state, pure economics have seen solar, wind, and battery installations roll out faster than in any other, save for California.

Solar now powers more Texan homes than coal, and installation records continue to be shattered.

The picture in Donald Trump's United States, much like the rest of the world, remains complex. Still, despite the best efforts of the "undisputed champion of beautiful clean coal", not everyone has been persuaded to stick with the black stuff.

title: 'They'll pay the price': Aussie travel hotspot's new tourist tax
text:
IN BRIEF Fiji tourism operators with a turnover above $1.3 million will be taxed 5 per cent from 1 September.

Australian and Fiji travel associations say they weren't consulted about the change and costs may be passed on to travellers with existing bookings.

The Fijian government will introduce a new tourism services tax for large-scale tourism operators next month, with travel industry experts warning that the costs could be passed on to customers.

The 5 per cent tax will apply from 1 September. The change has been criticised by travel associations in Fiji, Australia and New Zealand, who claim they were not properly consulted.

The Australian Travel Industry Association (ATIA) said the measure could catch out travellers who have already booked trips to Fiji from September onward, as travel agents and operators face confusion over how to administer the tax.

"The design and roll out reflect a complete lack of understanding of how the travel booking ecosystem works, and it is travellers and travel businesses who will pay the price for that failure," ATIA CEO Dean Long said.

"Travellers are the ones left exposed. Families with September school holiday bookings already paid in full, and travellers on large group, corporate and film production bookings, are being asked to find extra money for a holiday they thought was settled months ago. That is not how you treat people who chose Fiji in good faith."

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

The change forms part of wider taxation amendments enacted as part of Fiji's 2026-2027 national budget, passed last month.

It will affect tourism operators — including hotel, tourism and cruise businesses — with an annual turnover above FJ$2 million (approximately $1.3 million).

According to Fijian finance minister Esrom Immanuel, revenue from the tax will be used to support Fiji Airways.

"The revenue generated will be ring-fenced and fully directed to Fiji Airways, which continues to face financial pressure from rising aviation fuel costs and its ongoing recovery from losses incurred during the COVID-19 pandemic," Immanuel told local media in June.

It's reported that the tourism tax will generate around FJ$70 million ($44.7 million) for the airline. The Fijian government is the largest shareholder of Fiji Airways.

Consultation with Fijian government

ATIA confirmed it will meet with the Fijian government to discuss the tourism services tax, which it said arrived with "zero consultation".

Long said there is ongoing confusion over how the tax is collected, saying that members of the travel industry in Australia and New Zealand — which represent Fiji's largest tourism markets — were not consulted on the change.

"None of this needed to happen. The tax arrived with zero consultation with the travel industry in Australia or New Zealand despite the significant importance of these markets to Fiji," he said.

ATIA said there are still questions about how net rates (base prices which exclude discounts, commissions or fees) will be taxed, while the distinction between suppliers and agents remains "unresolved".

The Travel Agents' Association of New Zealand (TAANZ) said it was concerned with the way the tax is being implemented, and proposed that existing bookings be grandfathered.

"Grandfathering existing bookings is the fairest outcome. It protects travellers who purchased in good faith, gives the travel industry certainty and allows the new tax to be implemented cleanly for new bookings from 1 September," TAANZ CEO Julie White said.

SBS News has contacted the Fijian government's Ministry of Tourism for comment.

The number of Australians travelling to Fiji has remained stable in recent years. Source: Getty / ullstein bild

According to the Australian Bureau of Statistics, Fiji was one of the top 10 short-term return destinations for Australian travellers in June 2026.

Almost 37,000 Australians returned from short stays (less than one year) in Fiji in June this year. That's compared to around 35,000 visitors in June 2025.

In a statement issued in June, the Fiji Hotel and Tourism Association (FHTA) said the tourism industry did not propose, endorse or "broadly agree" to the tax.

FHTA CEO Fantasha Lockington added that retroactively adding costs would "undermine confidence in Fiji's tourism product".

"Operators cannot simply return to guests, agents or wholesalers to recover another 5 per cent without risking disputes, cancellations, destination and brand reputational damage or margin loss," she said, adding that industry operators do not agree to absorb the tax.

"Indications from members suggest the majority, if not all, will pass it on in its entirety," she said.

Lockington noted that Fiji Airways remains vital to the country's connectivity, visitor arrivals, trade and employment. However, she believes the carrier should be funded through a "national fiscal response", not a tax imposed on the travel sector.

In July, Immanuel told Fijian broadcaster FBC News he was "surprised" by FHTA's statement and claimed the proposal had received support during discussions before the budget.

title: After two decades, China is preparing its boldest Moon mission yet
text:
In brief China's next moon mission is expected to launch later this month.

Chang'e 7's unique mission will try to find frozen water on the moon's surface and see if it could be accessed.

How do you explore a place where the sun never shines? China's space program will soon embark on one of the most innovative lunar exploration missions in recent years.

We’ve known for nearly two decades that some form of water exists on the moon. What we still don’t know is exactly how much accessible water ice lies inside permanently shadowed craters, how deeply it is buried or what form it takes.

What we do know is that accessing that water ice will be a real challenge: it is found at the bottom of deep, hard-to-traverse craters where the sun never shines, remaining untouched for billions of years at temperatures well below –200C. These are among the most valuable places on the moon, but the hardest to reach and explore.

Lunar exploration has come a long way since the Soviet Union’s Luna-1 probe reached the moon's vicinity in January 1959. The Apollo missions and their successors showed the challenge is no longer simply to reach the moon. It is to explore places human and conventional rovers cannot easily go, and ultimately determine whether the moon itself can provide some of the resources that future explorers will need.

China has spent two decades building an increasingly ambitious lunar exploration program, named after Chang'e, the ancient Chinese goddess of the moon. The Chang'e-7 mission is expected to set course for our celestial neighbour later this month, although a recent failure involving a different Chinese rocket has introduced some uncertainty over the launch date. Here’s what makes this latest mission so interesting.

Enter email address Subscribe Morning (Mon–Fri) Afternoon (Mon–Fri) Weekend Insight By subscribing, you agree to SBS’s terms of service and privacy policy including receiving email updates from SBS.

What is Chang'e-7 set to achieve?

The mission will test several novel approaches to lunar exploration. It will consist of an orbiter, a lander, a rover and a hopper.

In addition, the Queqiao-2 lunar relay satellite is already in place. Launched separately in March 2024, it subsequently supported the Chang'e-6 mission and will facilitate communication between Earth and the lunar surface during the Chang'e-7 mission.

We don’t know precisely where the mission will land, but a site on or near an illuminated ridge close to the Shackleton crater in the Lunar South Pole’s Aitken region is a prime candidate.

The hopper will be the mission’s real star. Unlike a wheeled rover, it’s designed to leap over broken terrain and descend into craters where sunlight never reaches, places conventional vehicles may simply be unable to enter.

Adding it to the mission makes sense, given the steep crater walls, broken terrain, permanent shadow and the need for autonomous navigation and communications.

Chinese scientists won’t be looking for signs of water; we already have compelling evidence for lunar polar water. The question at the mission’s core is where exactly that water is located, in what form and concentration, and whether it could realistically be accessed.

This marks a transition from simply exploring the moon to determining whether its resources can actually be used.

How NASA is taking a different tack

Other nations are similarly interested in addressing that same question. The United States is pursuing the same longer-term objective of making sustained lunar operations possible. Although NASA will be confronted by the same physical problems, the American space agency has opted for a different solution.

Chang'e-7 is a coordinated state mission whose elements have been designed around a single, specific objective and which can use the already operational Queqiao-2 infrastructure.

NASA, by contrast, is deliberately trying something different: building a lunar marketplace through its Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) programme. The agency buys lunar delivery, mobility and technology services from companies that own and operate their own spacecraft.

NASA currently has 17 contracted deliveries carrying more than 60 instruments.

And the American effort has already yielded useful experience: Intuitive Machines’ IM-2 mission, Athena, attempted strikingly similar undertakings to Chang'e-7. It carried a drill and mass spectrometer looking for volatiles, a small hopping vehicle intended to explore difficult terrain and an experimental mobile communications network. However, the lander fell over at the landing site and was powered down just one day after arriving.

In essence, the destination dictates the problems; different space programmes are experimenting with different ways to resolve them.

Learning how to live on the moon

Finding lunar resources is only the first step. Chang'e-7 will attempt to determine where useful lunar resources are found near the moon's South Pole and characterise their nature.

Chang'e-8, slated for potential launch in 2028, will move towards demonstrating how they might actually be used.

Crewed exploration will likely follow, culminating in the construction of the International Lunar Research Station, jointly led by the China National Space Administration and Russia’s Roscosmos space agency.

On the other side of the Pacific, the CLPS will feed technology and science into the broader NASA-led Artemis program, which the agency explicitly describes as laying the foundation for sustained lunar exploration.

Ultimately, the lunar South Pole doesn’t care which flag is on a spacecraft. Any explorer entering its permanently shadowed craters faces the same darkness, severe cold, broken terrain and communications problems.

Getting to the moon was one of the great technological challenges of the 20th century. Learning how to live and work there may be one of the great challenges of the 21st.

title: Starc strikes early again as Bangladesh chase Australian lead on day two

Mackay: Australia will look to level the two-Test series with Bangladesh as early as Sunday, after a slice of Bangladeshi history ended the hosts’ first innings in the first session of day two with a commanding 146-run lead. It took a toe-crushing yorker from Shoriful Islam to end Cameron Green’s valiant lone hand with the bat, trapped in front on 67 as the left-arm seam bowler became Bangladesh’s first quick to claim seven wickets in a Test innings (7-48). Cameron Green was out leg before wicket in Australia’s first innings. Getty Images That milestone followed his nation’s first Test win on Australian soil in the first clash in Darwin. Green had looked composed throughout his innings until receiving the Shoriful peach, playing fluently until stumps on day one as wickets fell around him during a dramatic collapse of 5-30 from Steve Smith’s dismissal for 42.

Advertisement

The 27-year-old all-rounder appeared on track to back up his second innings 104 in the first Test in Darwin with a fourth career ton, playing one powerful cut shot and another elegant off-drive for boundaries inside the first three overs of day two at Great Barrier Reef Arena. When Green fell, Nathan Lyon ensured Australia moved beyond 200 – a well-timed on drive to the fence, and pull shot over it, featuring in his unbeaten 32 before Josh Hazlewood was out caught for six attempting to take on spinner Taijul Islam, ending Australia’s stand at 210. Bangladesh bowler Shoriful Islam celebrates his seven-wicket haul against Australia. Getty Images But Bangladesh were in early disarray when they came out to bat for the second time. While there were no repeats of Starc’s first-ball scalp on day one, Tanzid Hasan driving him down the ground to the boundary, the veteran quick did cause carnage in his second over. First, he caught Shadman Islam high on the bat with a sharp, straightening delivery, with Marnus Labuschagne diving forward from point for the catch. Next ball, the left-arm spearhead was on a hat-trick for the second time this Test, as Mominul Haque shouldered arms to a ball that nipped back and knocked out his off stump, to leave Bangladesh reeling at 2-5.

Advertisement

There were 18 wickets to fall on day one, Starc setting the tone by sealing his five-wicket haul after just 43-minutes, finishing with figures of 6-12 as the visitors struggled to contend with the extra bounce and lively green pitch. Despite the carnage, Starc said he had no issues with the pitch on Saturday. “People will sit there and go ’18 wickets, it’s a bad wicket’. I think it’s a very good day one wicket, I think it’s probably played very similar to a Gabba wicket – you see a little bit of tennis ball bounce early at the Gabba, and likewise today,” Starc said. “It was a pretty helter-skelter day of cricket, but I’d say some good bowling led to 18 wickets, as opposed to the wicket.” Should Starc and his fellow quicks roll Bangladesh in similar fashion, there will be no further chances for Labuschagne, Beau Webster and Matt Renshaw to push their case for inclusion in the forthcoming series in South Africa.

Advertisement

While Renshaw (eight) would be expected to be given a reprieve, having only just been brought into the side to replace axed opener Jake Weatherald, both Labuschagne and Webster have struggled for a more prolonged period. Webster, to his credit, had not put a foot wrong in his career until this two-Test series. However, he has managed just 17 runs across three knocks – including a first innings duck in Mackay. Labuschagne’s long-term struggles, meanwhile, have been well-documented – failing to score a century since July 2023, while averaging just 29.69 since the start of that year following his cheap dismissal for four on Saturday.

They will be there tomorrow for the first match day since the storm broke; first for the AFLW team’s clash against Essendon, then when the men’s team takes on North Melbourne. Bennett has been a Giants fan for 13 years but also supports the Swans, Sharp’s team. And I just think, you’ve done nothing wrong ... these kids, and the older players like Dane Rampe and Jake Lloyd who have been foot soldiers for them, and have played really well, they don’t deserve to not have fans there.”

However, she decided she wanted to support the players who weren’t involved in the scandal. “I spoke to my daughter who said it’s not the boys who are left behind’s fault, and if nobody goes, then that would be devastating,” Bennett said. Many, such as Emma Gray and her daughter, Esther, are only planning on attending the women’s match, from 12.30pm, before leaving ahead of the men’s game at 3.20pm.

Gray has been a Swans supporter for about 20 years, while her daughter backs Essendon, and was frustrated she couldn’t buy a ticket solely for the women’s match. “It’s a women’s match at a big venue which is definitely worth supporting for the promotion of the game,” Gray said. Emma Gray and her daughter Esther will be at the Swans AFLW match on Sunday. “We’re not staying for the men’s game because I don’t condone the misogynist culture which is clearly prevalent at the club. Why men, particularly in positions of privilege, think that celebrating with the ‘boys’ needs to involve demeaning women is absolutely beyond me.” Fans of rival clubs will also attend the SCG on Sunday, after the GWS Giants women’s team urged their supporters to turn up in solidarity.

“As we will be playing the Demons away from home in Melbourne, we would like to encourage our Sydney based and non-travelling fans, to continue supporting the spectacle of women’s football in Sydney by attending the match, before watching us play in Melbourne,” the Giants’ AFLW leadership team said in a statement. “This is a moment to put rivalries aside and bolster the women’s game in NSW by showing up and supporting the league and women in football.” ‘I’m going tomorrow because I really do feel sorry for the men, because they just look devastated. Her grandfather played for South Melbourne – the Swans’ origin club – in 1918. Carolyn Cummins has been a Swans supporter since she moved to Sydney in 1988. Cummins, a committee member for Ladies @ Sydney Swans – a fan group supported by the club that hosts events for female supporters, said both the men’s and women’s team needed their fans now more than ever. “I am a very proud Swans ambassador and I will certainly be there to support the AFLW team – I can’t wait to see how we perform throughout the season,” Cummins said.

title: The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map
text:

NationalNSWCity life The medal that will put Sydney on the map. The wrong map Julie Power August 23, 2026 — 9:03am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The Sydney Marathon scheduled for next Sunday has again put the city on the map, but maybe not the right map. When organisers of the TCS Sydney Marathon unveiled the official 2026 medal that is engraved with the major landmarks along the 42.2 km course past the Sydney Opera House, the Harbour Bridge and St Mary’s Cathedral, marathon runners spotted a detour that could add substantial distance … and time. Sydney Marathon competitors will get this medal, complete with various icons of the city’s landmarks … plus a surprise. Instagram Instead of including Sydney’s Allianz Stadium on Moore Park Road, Centennial Park, they included the Allianz Arena in Munich, Germany, some 16, 404 km away. To be fair, they do share some similarities: Both are round, large and designed to disguise their size. Munich’s stadium is made from inflated plastic panels, while Sydney’s Allianz Stadium was designed to resemble a cloud.

Advertisement

News of the error has made headlines around the world. The BBC reported that one week out from the world-renowned Sydney Marathon, organisers faced questions about whether designers etched the wrong city’s stadium on the participation medal. On Morning Coffee Run, a popular social media account, the error attracted hundreds of comments and likes. Host James Dunn said it was a major mess up. “Oh dear this is bad … Because someone Google-searched the wrong thing and got the Allianz Arena rather than the Allianz Stadium, which is in Sydney,” he said. The German Allianz Arena responded with humour. “Oh wow, we didn’t have that on our bingo card! 😂 Perhaps they tried to find something else they had in common: Allianz Arena_____Sydney Opera House. Unique Architecture ______ Both are worth a visit!” The error was uncovered after organisers unveiled its official 2026 medal, urging the public to look closely to “find the story of the course in the details”.

Advertisement

It is the second major blooper to embarrass organisers of a marathon. Runners at the 2012 Edinburgh Marathon were embarrassed when presented with what appeared to be a penis-shaped medal. Organisers of the Sydney Marathon said the markings around the edge represent each kilometre of the course, while the eight circles on the back represent the World Marathon Majors. “A beautiful Sydney skyline brings the course to life, featuring the landmarks runners will experience along the way — starting with the Sydney Harbour Bridge and finishing at the world-famous Sydney Opera House,” the Marathon’s official account said. Joggers running across the Sydney Harbour Bridge in the 2025 Sydney Marathon. Getty

Advertisement

Starting in North Sydney and then crossing the Sydney Harbour Bridge, an estimated 100,000 - 150,000 people are expected to watch the race. This masthead sought a response from the Marathon’s organisers, asking if the finisher medals would be scrapped and new ones issued. An automatic reply said: “This year, we are expecting a record 40,000 participants on the start line, alongside unprecedented interest from media, partners and stakeholders. Race week will also see new entertainment precincts, live sites and performances across the city, as well as initiatives supporting local businesses.” The Morning Edition newsletter is our guide to the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights. title: Aussie family's $1.6 million battle with council to reopen beloved free campsite: 'Ridiculous'
text:
An Aussie family says they won't back down without a fight after council conditions prevented their free campsite from reopening until they make upgrades estimated to cost a small fortune.

"Even if we won the Lotto tomorrow, it is not feasible," Kara O'Hara told Yahoo News.

The front paddock of the farm off a main road has been open to bush campers for about nine and a half years.

Kara explained that her parents offered the camping option after noticing tourists visiting Cobar had limited, cheap accommodation options.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Additionally, attracting tourists to Cobar also meant the local economy benefited, she added.

However, the Glen Hope Station site was prevented from operating after Cobar Shire Council approached the family to submit a development application for the campsite which was denied several times, Kara said.

The closure also derailed the family's discussions about future plans for the property, as the council advised the existing campground needed development approval before they could pursue them.

"We should be able to do whatever we wish to do with our land or have on our land," Kara insisted.

The Glen Hope Station Stay is found near the NSW opal town of White Cliffs, on the 77,000-acre working sheep farm. Source: Supplied

In pursuit of compliance, Kara claims the family spent thousands of dollars hiring professionals to help prepare applications and lodged several, which were rejected.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

So far, they have spent $25,000, she said.

"We've done everything possible from here onwards to try and be compliant, jumping through the hurdles."

RELATED:

The fight with the council has lasted over a year.

Cobar Shire Council reportedly said that if it finds people staying at the campsite when it is supposed to be closed, the property owners will be fined $3,000 for individuals or $6,000 for a corporation.

What needs to happen to reopen campsite?

Cobar Shire Council confirmed it has since approved a development application, but only under certain conditions.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

Those conditions require:

The campsite to upgrade to compostable toilets for campers

And for Barrier Highway, where campers turn into the campsite, to include a Basic Right Turn and Basic Left Turn intersection treatment, including widened and sealed pavement, line marking, signage, and associated roadworks.

It's the cost of adhering to the road conditions that Kara argues is especially unfair for the family to bear solely.

She explained the estimated cost would be far beyond what the family could recover from operating a low-cost campsite.

"It is unfeasible, it's unlawful, it's ridiculous," she said, estimating the upgrades will cost between $1.2 million to $1.6 million.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"We don't own the road," she insisted.

The family is questioning why they should carry the full financial burden of the highway works, suggesting government or tourism funding could provide an alternative.

In an emailed statement toYahoo, the council said the applicant's traffic consultant concluded the intersection upgrades are needed.

A Transport for NSW spokesperson said the department had agreed the intersection work must be completed before the campsite can operate again.

Despite the campground remaining closes, Kara said her family does not intend to abandon its efforts in finding a solution with local and state governments. Source: Supplied

Family 'won't give up' on campsite

The campsite was never opened to generate profit, but to create a safe and affordable place for travellers to stop in Cobar, Kara insists.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

She said local businesses have also expressed their support for the campground, as they are concerned travellers will no longer stop in town without access to the campsite.

"We're not going to give up," Kara said, as she hopes council, the state authority, and her family can agree to reopen the free bush campsite without imposing costs on the family.

title: ‘Tilt my hat’: One Nation’s unlikely alliance
text:
One Nation MP David Farley has confirmed the federal government will provide a multimillion-dollar package to support SunRice mills in the NSW Riverina after an intervention from Anthony Albanese.

SunRice, one of the largest rice companies in the world, revealed earlier this month it would cull 78 jobs and change 92 positions across its Deniliquin and Leeton mills, as well as Australian Grain Storage.

SunRice chief executive Paul Serra, in a statement announcing the changes, highlighted the company would continue to advocate against the "adverse impacts of water policy settings" on the rice industry in the Riverina.

SunRice will receive a multi-million government handout to keep its Riverina operations going. Picture: Supplied

The government's controversial water buyback scheme has been blamed by critics, including Mr Farley, for reducing the amount of irrigation water available for growing crops, and thus lowering crop volumes.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

But in a Sunday appearance on ABC Insiders, Mr Farley said a deal to save the SunRice jobs had been struck.

"I'm happy with the outcome as it's progressing," he said.

The Farrer MP said the Prime Minister had approached him at an event earlier in the week and pledged support from the government.

"I was impressed how (Mr Albanese) at the Governor-General's event the other night, came straight up to me and said, 'Look, I'm aware of it. I'm working on it. We'll get it done,'" Mr Farley said.

David Farley says Anthony Albanese approached him about the SunRice issue. Picture: NewsWire / Martin Ollman

"Even after, as we left the (House of Representatives) chamber the other day, we spoke, all the way across to the Senate, talking about it. How (the support) could be done and put together.

Advertisement Advertisement

Advertisement Advertisement

"So you know, I tilt my hat to them."

Though he did not confirm details of the deal, Mr Farley said he had previously lobbied the government to match the $15m provided by the industry to invest in the plant "to avoid the redundancies of 78 families".

As for his position on the water buybacks, Mr Farley said local producers had concerns the policy was prioritising the environment over food security.

"We're great proponents and believers that you know you need a healthy food chain, affordable, secure food, and you need a healthy environment," he said.

The Agriculture Minister's office has been contacted for comment.
